The Pile on the Table

There’s a particular kind of evening when the decision has been circling for months and hasn’t been made yet. The mail has stacked up on the end of the table because neither of you has been opening it with any real attention — an account statement, a mortgage statement, a letter from a plan administrator you don’t recognize anymore. You sit down with the stack, meaning to sort it, and instead you just look at it. You haven’t said the sentence out loud yet, and you notice that not saying it is its own kind of work, heavier than the sorting.

Leave the pile where it is tonight. Tomorrow, you can decide which paper needs an answer first. What I want you to sit with here is just the shape of the evening: an unmade decision, a pile of paper that suddenly matters more than it did yesterday, and no idea yet which piece of it to pick up first.

That not-knowing is the reason this book exists.

Why this is a different problem at this age

Here is the plain version: divorcing at fifty-five is not divorcing at thirty with more wrinkles. It is a different financial problem, and treating it like the same one is how people lose money they can’t get back.

At thirty, you mostly have time on your side. Whatever gets divided, there are still twenty or thirty working years ahead to rebuild it. At fifty or sixty, that runway is short, and it keeps getting shorter while the paperwork grinds through the courts. A bad year in the market or a year lost to a stalled filing doesn’t have the same decades behind it to smooth out. You feel every delay in a way a younger couple doesn’t.

There’s a second difference, and it’s the one most people underestimate going in. After twenty, thirty, thirty-five years together, the money isn’t sitting in one checking account you both watch. It’s spread across old 401(k)s from jobs neither of you has held in a decade, a pension from a company that may not even use that name anymore, and an IRA opened after a rollover nobody remembers filling out. Add a brokerage account with decades of appreciation baked into it, and a house that’s been “paid off” so long you stopped thinking of it as an asset with a cost attached. Untangling that takes more than a conversation. It takes documents, and sometimes it takes professionals, and it almost always takes longer than you’d like.

In some marriages, retirement accounts may be worth more than the equity in the house. Put both amounts on the same balance sheet before negotiating either one. The house is the asset you can walk through, touch, and picture selling, which is exactly why it tends to dominate the conversation at the kitchen table. A 401(k) statement is a column of numbers mailed once a quarter; it doesn’t have a front porch or a kitchen you renovated together. That difference in how an asset feels has nothing to do with how much it’s actually worth, and trading away a share of a retirement account because the house feels like the bigger prize is one of the costliest mistakes this book can help you avoid. I’m going to ask you, more than once in this book, to look past the room you’re standing in and toward the accounts you can’t see from where you’re standing.

What this book is for

This book is a sequence, not a textbook on family law and not a substitute for the professionals you’re going to need. It starts with two decisions: what to gather before you agree to anything, and how a retirement account actually gets divided. Everything else follows from those.

If a signing deadline or a coverage lapse is already in front of you, call your attorney today; the section below tells you what to ask. If nothing is due this week, start with Chapter 10’s account inventory before any other chapter.

Each chapter ends with something you can use — a checklist, a worksheet, a set of questions — built to hand to your attorney or your CPA rather than to argue with them. I’d rather give you the right question to ask a professional than a half-confident answer that might not hold up in your state.

What this book is not

I am not a lawyer, a CPA, a financial planner, or a mediator, and I don’t pretend to be one in these pages. Carol Dunn is a pen-name voice. The situations in these pages are composites, not evidence that their author went through a divorce. Use the questions here with your own attorney or CPA. Nothing in this book is legal, tax, or financial advice, and nothing in it creates any kind of professional relationship with you. Divorce law, property division, and support rules vary by state, and retirement plan terms vary by plan. Where that matters — and it matters often — I’ll say so, name the source that governs the general rule, and tell you how to confirm the version that applies to you.

There are two subjects this book touches but does not try to finish. Social Security has a divorced-spouse rule worth knowing early, and I will give you the short version when it comes up, with a pointer to Social Security, Claimed On Purpose for the full claiming-age strategy. Medicare belongs to its own book entirely, Medicare Made Plain, and I will mention it only once, near the chapter on health coverage. I would rather hand you a whole book on each than squeeze a thin version into this one.

If something is due this week

Before you read another page, check whether you are actually facing a deadline right now, because that changes what you do tonight. Not every piece of paper in your pile is a deadline. Most of it is background. But a few kinds of notice need an answer on a clock, and it’s worth learning to tell them apart before you decide what to read next.

A court or signing deadline looks like a date on a filing, a settlement agreement, or a letter from your attorney’s office telling you a response is due by a certain day. If you have one of these, it takes priority over every chapter in this book. Call your attorney today, not after you’ve finished gathering records, and ask what this specific date requires of you. Ask your attorney which documents this specific deadline requires. Do not assume it calls for either your whole file or a short list.

If coverage through a spouse’s employer may end soon, read Chapter 16 before any other chapter and ask the plan administrator, in writing, for the date coverage ends and every notice or election deadline that applies to you.

An account-access deadline shows up when a joint account, a joint credit card, or a shared line of credit is being closed, frozen, or converted as part of the separation. If a letter or a conversation tells you a joint account will close or change on a specific date, that date matters more than any chapter order in this book. Before that date arrives, know which bills are set to draft from that account and have a plan for where they’ll draft from afterward. A missed mortgage or utility payment during a transition doesn’t care whose fault the paperwork delay was.

A lender deadline is the one people most often discover too late. If your name is on a mortgage, a refinance, or a loan being restructured as part of the settlement, the lender sets its own window to complete that change. A settlement may set a refinance deadline. The lender may set a different deadline for its own approval process. Ask your attorney how the two dates interact.

If you’ve read these four kinds of deadlines and none of them describe anything in your pile right now, you likely have more room than it feels like tonight. That doesn’t mean the pile isn’t urgent in its own way. It means the urgency is about getting organized, not about beating a clock — and that’s exactly the problem the next chapter is built to solve.

Whichever kind of deadline you’re facing, write down four things before you call anyone. Note the exact date on the notice. Note the name and phone number of the person or office it came from. Note the specific action it’s asking you to take. Then write one question for your attorney: is that action actually required of you right now. Keep that note on top of the pile, not in your head. A written note is the first thing your attorney’s office will ask for when you call, often before they ask for any other document.

How to use this book

Read it roughly in order, at least the first few chapters. The early chapters on gathering records and understanding how retirement accounts divide set up almost everything that comes after — the house, the debt, the taxes, the budget you’ll eventually build. If a specific chapter matches a decision in front of you right now, you can skip ahead to it, but go back and read what you skipped before you sign anything. The beneficiary chapter is later in the sequence; if you are updating accounts now, read it before you sign or submit any forms.

Keep a notebook or a document open as you go. Several chapters build worksheets meant to be filled in over weeks, not read once and closed. The account-and-document checklist you’ll build in the next chapter, in particular, is worth revisiting every time a new piece of paper turns up, because it will.

And when a chapter tells you to ask an attorney or a CPA a specific question, write the question down verbatim and bring it to the appointment. Ask how the appointment is billed, and bring a written list of questions and documents.

One honest thing before we start

One household may have less money to work with after divorce, while some costs will not fall in half. Build a budget from your own post-divorce income, obligations and housing costs before accepting a settlement. The job in front of you isn’t to guess at that number. It’s to make sure that when the dividing happens, it happens on terms you understood, with records you kept, and with nothing important left unsigned, unasked, or forgotten on a form you haven’t looked at in years.

Start with the pile on the table. The next chapter tells you exactly what to do with it.

Chapter 10: The Pile Becomes a List

I sat at that kitchen table with the decaf going cold and realized I could not have told anyone, with a straight face, how many bank accounts I had. Not the number. Not the names on them. I knew the building where we banked — a squat brick branch off Baseline Road I’d driven past twice a week for fifteen years — and that was it.

It took me two weeks of phone calls, old emails, and one afternoon going through a filing cabinet Russ hadn’t locked, to learn the real number. Six. A checking account and a savings account we both used. A 401(k) from the utility company. A second 401(k) from a job he’d held in the nineties that I’d never once heard him mention. An IRA that had apparently absorbed that old 401(k) in a rollover nobody told me about. And a pension, vested, that I only found because a statement for it showed up in March with his name misspelled.

Six. After thirty-one years. I’ll say this plainly, because nobody said it to me: you do not know what you own until you’ve gone and counted it, and counting it is the first job, before any lawyer, before any conversation about who gets the house.

Before you agree to anything, get the statements

Here is the only rule in this chapter that matters more than the rest: do not sign anything, agree to anything verbally, or let a conversation about “how we’ll split things” go further than small talk until you have copies of every account statement you can find. Not because you’re plotting something. Because you cannot negotiate over money you can’t see, and a spouse who has run the finances for three decades knows where everything is in a way you may not.

This isn’t paranoia. It’s homework, and it’s homework nobody assigns you. A family-law attorney will ask for this list in your first real meeting. If you show up with it already built, that meeting does actual work instead of spending its first hour on an inventory you could have brought.

Start with records for accounts you own or jointly own, and documents you may lawfully access. Do not enter an account or use a login that is not yours. Ask your attorney how to request records for anything else.

Checking and savings accounts, joint and individual. Even the account you forgot existed, the one with forty dollars in it from a tax refund three years ago, goes on the list. It’s not about the forty dollars. It’s about training yourself to assume nothing.

Retirement accounts — 401(k), 403(b), 457, IRA, Roth IRA, SEP-IRA, any pension. If either of you has worked for more than one employer, there may be an old plan sitting untouched from a job neither of you talks about anymore. That’s exactly the kind of account that gets missed, and exactly the kind that can hold real money.

Brokerage and investment accounts, including anything at a firm you don’t recognize from a financial advisor who called once in 2011 and set something up.

Life insurance policies with any cash value, and annuities.

Real estate — the house you live in, and anything else: a rental, a timeshare, land out of state, a cabin that’s been “in the family” but is actually titled to one of you.

Debt — every credit card, car loan, personal loan, home equity line, and anything cosigned. Debt counts in this inventory exactly as much as assets do, because what you owe shapes what you can actually walk away with.

Business interests, if either of you owns part of a company, a practice, or even a small side business that files its own return.

Get this from your own files first. Later in this chapter I’ll walk you through pulling a credit report, which is often where a hidden account turns up on paper, in your name, whether anyone meant for you to see it or not.

What “discovery” means, in plain terms

Somewhere in this process, probably from your attorney, you’ll hear the word “discovery.” It sounds more dramatic than it is. Discovery is the formal legal process by which each spouse is required to disclose financial information — accounts, income, debts, property — to the other, under rules that vary by state and by court. It exists because the law assumes, correctly in a lot of long marriages, that one spouse may know far more about the money than the other, and that a fair settlement requires both of you working from the same facts.

You do not need to understand the mechanics of discovery to start building your own list tonight. What you need to know is simpler: the list you’re building now, from your own records, before any formal request goes out, gives your attorney a head start. It also gives you a way to check whether what eventually comes through discovery matches what you already know. State law varies on what each spouse must disclose and when, so ask your attorney, early, what your state requires and what happens if an asset turns up that wasn’t on anyone’s list.

The checklist

By the end of my second week, I had a single sheet of paper taped inside a kitchen cabinet, out of sight but not out of reach. It had every account I’d found, with four columns: the institution, the account type, the approximate balance as of my most recent statement, and whose name was on it. I added to it every time a new piece of mail turned up, and new mail did turn up, for months.

Build the same sheet. One row per account or debt, with the institution and account type, the approximate balance as of your most recent statement, whose name is on it, and where the statement or confirmation is filed — a folder, a scanned copy, a photo on your phone of the screen.

Keep a copy somewhere your spouse doesn’t control and doesn’t know to look — a folder at a sibling’s house, a cloud account only you can access, a safe deposit box in your name alone if you have one. I kept mine, eventually, at my brother Ed’s place in Albuquerque, which felt a little like something out of a spy novel and was really just common sense.

The account-and-document checklist

For each account or debt category below, record: institution, last four digits of the account number, owner or title (yours, spouse’s, or joint), balance and date of the statement, whether the statement is saved, your access status, your question for the attorney, and your next action.

  • Bank accounts, checking and savings
  • Workplace and individual retirement plans, plus any pension
  • Brokerage and investment holdings
  • Policies with cash value, and annuities
  • Property you own, live in, or hold title to
  • Every debt, owed alone or together
  • Any share of a business or practice

Request your credit reports, and consider a freeze

Request all three at AnnualCreditReport.com; compare each report because the information can differ. You’re looking for two things: accounts you didn’t know existed, and activity — new cards, new inquiries — that’s happened recently without your knowledge. For a freeze, you’ll still contact Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion separately.

A credit report can reveal credit accounts, loans, and inquiries you did not recognize. It will not reliably show retirement accounts. Use old tax returns, W-2s, employer records, mail, and formal disclosure to look for those.

A credit freeze is worth understanding here, even if you decide not to use one yet. According to the Federal Trade Commission, a security freeze is free and stays in place until you lift it. It does not affect your credit score. And it must be requested separately with each of the three nationwide bureaus, since freezing one does not freeze the others.

A freeze stops new creditors from checking your credit, which stops most new accounts from being opened in your name without your knowledge. It won’t affect existing joint accounts you’re already on, and it won’t retroactively undo anything that’s already open. If you’re worried about new debt being taken out during a contentious separation, a freeze is a reasonable, reversible step. It costs you nothing but the paperwork of lifting it later, if you need to apply for credit yourself before the freeze comes off.

Separate the joint cards you can

Once you have your list, look specifically at the joint credit cards and any shared line of credit. If you are a joint borrower, the account agreement may leave each borrower responsible for charges; an authorized user may have different rights and liability. Call the issuer, review the agreement, and ask your attorney what you may change while the case is pending. We’ll cover the deeper question of joint debt, and what a decree can and can’t do about it, in Chapter 14. For now, the practical step is simpler: where you can, close joint cards you no longer need jointly. Open an individual account in your own name too, if you don’t already have one, so you have a credit history that isn’t tied to a marriage that’s ending.

Don’t close every joint account reflexively before talking to your attorney, especially if doing so could look like you’re trying to freeze your spouse out of shared funds during a dispute. Courts in some states take a dim view of a spouse who moves money or closes credit unilaterally right before or during a filing. This is one of the places where a quick phone call to your attorney before you act can help you avoid a mistake that may be hard to undo. Ask specifically whether closing a given joint account now could complicate your case.

A temporary budget, built fast and rough

You don’t need a polished budget this week. You need a rough one, built in an evening, that tells you two things. What’s coming in, from any source. And what has to go out no matter what happens with the divorce — the mortgage or rent, utilities, insurance premiums, minimum debt payments, groceries. List those in one column. In a second column, write what you’re actually spending now, which is often a different number. The gap between those two columns is the thing you and your attorney need to know before any temporary support arrangement gets discussed. A judge or a mediator can’t account for a shortfall nobody mentioned.

This isn’t the single-person budget you’ll build later, in Chapter 20, once the settlement is closer to final. This is a bridge budget — a way to see clearly for the next few months while everything else is still being sorted out. Write it on paper or in a plain spreadsheet. You don’t need software for this, and you don’t need it to be pretty. You need it to be honest.

When to call your attorney now, not later

A few situations in this chapter are urgent enough that they shouldn’t wait for you to finish the full inventory. If you believe an account has been emptied, moved, or hidden in the weeks since the decision to divorce became real, tell your attorney immediately. Don’t wait to see if the money reappears, and don’t confront your spouse about it yourself before you’ve talked to counsel. State law varies on what counts as improper dissipation of marital assets and what a court can do about it, but the window to act matters.

If you’re being asked to sign anything — a temporary agreement, a line on a joint account closure, anything — before you’ve finished your own inventory, slow down and call your attorney first. And if you genuinely don’t know whether an asset belongs to you, your spouse, or both, write the question down. Bring it to your first real meeting rather than guessing an answer into the conversation.

Your list is the starting point, not the division. Next, use the retirement-account entries to learn what a plan needs before it can divide them.

Chapter 11: What a Plan Actually Needs

My attorney told me, back when the decree was still a draft, that the hard part was behind us. We’d agreed on a number. Russ would keep the house and his pension; I’d get half of his 401(k) from the utility company, plus the old one from the nineties job. Each award was written as a percentage of the account when the plan implemented the division. On paper, it looked settled. It took four more months before a dollar of it moved. During the delay, the account fell nearly ten percent, so the dollar value of my percentage fell with it. The decree said what it said, but our process had missed the plan’s instructions.

That gap — between what a judge signs and what a retirement plan actually does — is the single most expensive thing I didn’t understand going into this. I want to close it for you now, before you’re the one waiting on a letter.

What’s actually divisible: state law decides, not you

Before any of this reaches a plan, someone has to work out what share of an account is marital or community property and what share is separate. That answer turns on your state’s law, not a formula you can run yourself from a statement balance. The marriage date, the separation or filing date, when contributions were made, and years of service all matter, and they interact differently depending on where you live. Give your attorney the marriage date, the separation or filing date, and each account’s contribution and service history, and let state-licensed counsel determine what’s actually yours to divide.

Your decree doesn’t talk to the plan by itself

Here’s the belief I walked in with, and I suspect you might be carrying some version of it too. Once the judge signs the divorce decree awarding me half of Russ’s 401(k), I figured the money was mine, more or less automatically. It isn’t automatic. The decree alone usually isn’t enough.

Many private-employer 401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing and pension plans are governed by ERISA and use a QDRO. Governmental, church and other plans may use different domestic-relations-order rules. Ask each plan administrator, in writing, which law and order process govern that specific plan. For the plan to pay out any part of a participant’s benefit to a spouse or former spouse, it needs a particular kind of order: a Qualified Domestic Relations Order, almost always shortened to QDRO. Per IRS Publication 504, a QDRO is a judgment, decree, or court order, including an approved property settlement agreement, issued under a state’s or tribe’s domestic relations law. It recognizes someone’s right to receive all or part of a participant’s benefit, and it contains the specific terms the plan requires.

Notice what that definition doesn’t say. It doesn’t say the order has to be a separate document from the decree. An approved property settlement agreement can itself be a QDRO if it contains the required terms. What it does require is that the right document, with the right language, reaches the right office: not the courthouse, not your attorney’s file cabinet, but the plan administrator. The plan administrator, not the family-court judge, makes the qualification determination. Your attorney can draft something airtight by every standard a family court cares about. A plan can still reject it if it doesn’t match that plan’s own requirements. This isn’t the court overruling itself. It’s two different systems — state domestic-relations law, and a federally governed retirement plan — that don’t automatically read each other’s paperwork.

An IRA is different, and worth separating out here so you don’t carry the QDRO rule where it doesn’t belong. An IRA isn’t an employer plan, and ERISA’s QDRO machinery doesn’t apply to it. Under Publication 504, moving all or part of an IRA to an ex-spouse because of a divorce decree, or a written instrument incident to one, isn’t a taxable event. An IRA transfer incident to divorce must follow the decree or qualifying written instrument and the custodian’s procedures. A direct custodian-to-custodian transfer is usually the clean route; do not withdraw the money personally. Ask the custodian and a tax professional how to document it. Go back to the list you built in Chapter 10. If every row on it is an IRA, this chapter’s central warning doesn’t apply to you the same way, though the tax treatment below still does. If any row is a 401(k), a 403(b), a 457, or a pension, keep reading closely.

Six things you can actually control

I spent those four months calling my attorney’s office every couple of weeks, asking some version of “is it done yet,” and getting some version of “it’s in process” back. What I didn’t know then, and wish I had, is that there was no clock running that either of us could read. Plan processing times vary by plan. No official source states a typical number of weeks, and I won’t invent one for you here. What you can do instead is control the sequence, in order, so that nothing sits waiting on a step nobody started.

First, request the plan’s written QDRO procedures. ERISA requires retirement plans to maintain written procedures for determining whether an order is qualified, and many plans also offer model order language built to match what they need. Your attorney, or you, can request this directly from the plan administrator. Find that contact in the plan’s summary plan description, the online participant portal, a recent plan notice, or the plan’s Form 5500 filing. It may be an employer committee or a third-party administrator, not the HR desk you’d expect; confirm the submission address in writing. Do this early, ideally as soon as you know which accounts are in play, not after the decree is signed. I didn’t learn this document existed until my attorney mentioned it almost as an afterthought, three months in, and the time it had sat unrequested was time nobody got back.

Second, have the order drafted against those procedures. This usually means your attorney, or an outside specialist your attorney brings in for exactly this task, writes the QDRO to match the plan’s own required terms. Make sure the draft specifies the valuation date, whether the award is a fixed dollar amount or a percentage, how gains and losses are allocated between the valuation date and the transfer, any outstanding plan loans, and contributions made after the cutoff. Those terms, not the processing time, decide whether a delay costs you anything. It can happen alongside the decree, or shortly after, rather than waiting for the decree to finalize first and starting from scratch. The two documents can move in parallel. Ask your attorney directly whether that’s happening in your case, because it’s an easy step to let slide while everyone’s attention is on the decree itself.

Third, submit the draft to the plan for preapproval, if the plan offers it. Many plans will review an unsigned draft informally and flag problems before it’s final. An unsigned draft never gets qualified on its own, but catching mistakes early saves a formal resubmission later.

Fourth, once the decree is entered, promptly send the plan the signed or certified order it requires. A draft sitting in a file folder, preapproved or not, does nothing until the executed order the plan asked for actually reaches it.

Fifth, get the administrator’s written qualification determination. The plan reviews the order against its own procedures and tells you, in writing, whether it qualifies. If it doesn’t, you’ll get specific reasons, and the order goes back for revision. This is a normal part of the process, not a sign anything has gone wrong. It is, though, one more reason to start the sequence early rather than late, since a resubmission costs time you don’t get back.

Sixth, confirm in writing that the division was actually implemented. A qualified order and an executed transfer are not the same thing. Ask the plan to confirm, in writing, that your share has been set up as its own account or recorded in the plan’s records. This is the step I’d tell you never to skip, because “qualified” only means the plan accepted the order’s terms. It doesn’t mean the money has moved.

None of these six steps comes with a promised number of weeks attached, and I’m not going to invent one for you. What I can tell you is that every month this sequence sits untouched is a month the account keeps doing whatever the market does, with nobody’s name clearly attached to the piece that’s supposed to be yours.

What happened to mine, and what I’d do differently

The old 401(k) from the nineties job — the one I didn’t know existed until Chapter 10’s search turned it up — is the one that cost me. My attorney drafted the order, but nobody requested the plan’s written procedures first. The draft came back twice for revisions that could have been caught the first time, if we’d started with what the plan actually required. By the time the administrator confirmed the division was implemented, the market had dropped, and my half was a smaller number in dollars than it would have been the week the decree was signed. Because the order fixed my share as a percentage of the account rather than a dollar amount, my share was calculated against that lower balance, and the drop came straight out of what I actually received.

I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to turn this into a bigger lesson than it actually supports. I don’t know what the market would have done if the order had moved in half the time. It might have dropped anyway. What I do know is that nobody was watching the clock on that account while two other things moved faster. The gap between signing and dividing is a real risk sitting in the account the whole time it’s open, in either direction — it can cut against you or in your favor, and you have no control over which. If I were doing this again, I would ask, on day one, for the plan’s QDRO procedures on every workplace account on my list, before the decree was anywhere close to final. That’s the one piece of this chapter I’d go back and hand to myself.

A pension complicates this further, because a pension’s QDRO often needs to address survivor benefits too, not just the dollar split.

What happens to the money once it moves

If part of your share comes to you directly rather than rolling into your own retirement account, Publication 504 treats it as generally included in your income for tax purposes. You have two real choices, and a CPA should weigh in before you pick one. Take it as cash, and it’s taxable income now, usually with 20 percent withheld automatically. Or roll it, as an eligible rollover distribution, tax-free into an IRA or another qualified plan, where it becomes your own retirement money. There’s one more reason to ask a CPA first. A distribution paid to you as an alternate payee under a QDRO is an exception to the 10 percent early-distribution tax that otherwise applies under age 59 1/2 (see the IRS’s retirement-topics page on tax on early distributions). That exception belongs to the QDRO payout itself; it doesn’t carry over to a later withdrawal from the IRA you roll it into. Ask the plan, before any money moves, whether your share can go by direct rollover rather than as a check made out to you, and ask your CPA which choice fits your situation. A check you deposit yourself still has rollover rules and a limited window to act; a direct, trustee-to-trustee rollover avoids that and the automatic withholding.

This is also the moment to decide, with a CPA if the number is large enough to matter, whether you want this money in its own account, separate from anything else. A clean record of what came from the QDRO, and when, is worth having. Chapter 19 will ask you to update every beneficiary form you touch; that includes this new account, from the day it opens.

Questions for your attorney, written down before you call

Bring these, verbatim, to the attorney handling your case. Don’t paraphrase them into the conversation and hope the right answer comes back; ask them as written.

Which of our accounts need a QDRO, and which are IRAs that only need a custodian-to-custodian transfer? Is the QDRO being drafted alongside the decree, or will it wait until after the decree is final? Once drafted, how will it be submitted, and who is responsible for following up with the plan if we don’t hear back? When the plan sends its written qualification determination, will you send me a copy, and will you also confirm, separately, that the division was actually implemented in the account records?

Before you move on

One more thing worth saying plainly: none of this is a reason to delay the decision itself. The QDRO sequence runs on its own timeline, alongside the rest of the case, not after it. Plenty of divorces finalize with the order still moving through a plan’s review. Do not assume that starting the process preserves every right. Ask your attorney and the plan, before the decree or any retirement election, which steps must be completed to protect the award and survivor rights in your case.

Mark, right now, which accounts on your Chapter 10 list are workplace plans and which are IRAs. For every workplace plan, call your attorney’s office today, not to ask whether it’s done yet, but to ask whether the plan’s written QDRO procedures have been requested. That single call is the one that would have saved me the most, if I’d known to make it four months earlier than I did. The next chapter takes the pension specifically, and the survivor-benefit question a QDRO alone doesn’t answer.

Chapter 12: The Pension Question I Hadn’t Asked

Celia stopped with her pen above the paragraph about Russ’s pension. I had been looking at the division of property, checking whether the draft said what I thought we’d agreed. She was looking for something else: what the papers said about a pension survivor benefit for me.

I couldn’t answer her. I hadn’t known that was a separate question.

In my head, letting Russ keep the pension meant there was nothing left for me to understand. Celia wanted to know whether the agreement also gave up a possible payment after his death, and whether we’d checked the plan’s rules. We weren’t choosing an answer yet.

That distinction matters. It is possible to agree about retirement income while leaving the death provision unread. I would have done it quite calmly, with my glasses on.

A monthly amount has conditions attached

The Department of Labor’s Types of Retirement Plans explains that a defined benefit pension promises a specified retirement benefit, which may be calculated from salary and service. A 401(k), by contrast, is a defined contribution account: its value reflects contributions and investment results. The pension paragraph in your agreement therefore needs more than the sort of balance-and-percentage discussion you used in Chapter 11.

Here, pension means that defined benefit promise. Ask the administrator what kind of plan you have. The Labor Department identifies cash balance pensions as defined benefit plans too, even though their statements can display an account-style balance.

An estimate of monthly income needs a date and a payment form beside it. Ask whether it assumes the employee stops working now or continues earning service, and whether it assumes payments begin at a particular retirement age. Ask whether it is payable only during the employee’s life or includes payments after death. These aren’t details to fill in after you compare offers. They tell you what the offer contains.

Bring the service dates from your Chapter 10 inventory, without trying to calculate your legal share from them. State law varies and determines the divisible marital or community interest; plan terms and pension law determine how an award can be paid. Have your attorney identify the governing state rule and its official statute or court guidance. My Arizona divorce is not a formula for yours.

A monthly estimate is also not a lump sum you can subtract from a brokerage balance. If someone proposes that you give up a pension interest in exchange for another asset, have an independent pension valuation professional examine the proposal with your attorney. Timing, payment conditions and death protection affect that comparison. Simple multiplication cannot price a lifetime promise.

While alive and after death are different promises

A pension survivor benefit is a payment to someone else after the employee dies. The Labor Department’s QDROs: The Division of Retirement Benefits Through Qualified Domestic Relations Orders, in its drafting chapter, treats retirement benefits and survivor benefits separately for exactly this reason. Dividing the first does not answer how the second should be assigned.

There are two death situations to check: death before retirement payments begin, and death after they begin. Protection in one situation is not an answer about the other. Ask the administrator to describe both in writing, using the actual plan documents, not a general benefits brochure.

The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation gives a useful, concrete explanation in its Drafting a QDRO guidance, updated April 23, 2026. For pensions it administers as trustee, it describes a qualified pre-retirement survivor annuity, or QPSA, for death before payments start. It also describes a qualified joint-and-survivor annuity, or QJSA, whose survivor portion concerns death after payments start. You don’t need to speak in those initials. You do need to recognize which situation the document is addressing.

PBGC also explains that a QDRO can assign all or part of available survivor benefits to a former spouse. It tells readers to establish who is already entitled and to address the assignment expressly in the decree and the QDRO. A sentence dividing monthly retirement payments should not be treated as confirmation that survivor protection has been arranged.

PBGC’s implementation guidance applies to plans it has taken over as trustee, not every pension. Your administrator must identify the provisions and requirements in your plan. The ERISA scope distinction from Chapter 11 still applies; governmental and church plans may follow different rules.

Nor should you assume divorce erases an existing survivor election, or assume that it preserves one. The PBGC guidance warns that earlier elections, waivers and spousal consents can affect who is entitled. Give counsel those documents, including any order involving another former spouse. Ask what divorce changes under the law and the plan that actually govern you.

The beneficiary-form sweep in Chapter 19 is a different task. Don’t substitute a new form for resolving the pension rights in the settlement.

Sharing a payment or receiving a separate interest

The words used to divide a pension can describe quite different arrangements. PBGC’s 2026 drafting guidance explains a shared payment approach and a separate interest approach. Use these as names for questions, not as instructions to select an option without the plan’s answer.

Under a shared payment arrangement, your award comes from the employee’s payments as they are made. The practical question is what happens if those payments have not started, or stop. For a PBGC-trusteed pension, its guidance says you receive no shared retirement payments if the participant never begins receiving benefits. Survivor provisions must be examined separately. Don’t budget as though an expected retirement date is confirmed.

A separate interest arrangement gives you an independent right to an assigned portion of the retirement benefit. PBGC explains that this can allow a different starting time and payment form from the employee’s, within its rules. It is not permission to take the benefit whenever you please, and it is not automatically a cash account that you can withdraw.

There is a sharp timing limit in PBGC’s example: a separate interest QDRO is not available after the participant begins receiving benefits from PBGC. Once payments have started, PBGC can qualify only a shared payment approach. Other administrators must explain their own permissible arrangements and restrictions. Ask which choices are still open in your case before you negotiate around one of them.

Have the person drafting your pension order explain, in ordinary language, whose life controls the duration of your payments. Then ask what happens if you die first, if the employee dies first, and if either death occurs before your payments begin. Even with a separate interest, the treatment before your benefit starts needs checking. “Independent” is not an answer to every death question.

The QDRO process you learned in Chapter 11 carries the award into the plan. It doesn’t choose these terms for you. The pension-specific job is making sure the order addresses the payment arrangement, its start and end, and any survivor rights you intend to secure.

Read the smaller monthly quote before rejecting it

A payment form that includes survivor protection can have a different monthly amount from one without it. Ask for written estimates of the available forms on the same assumptions. Don’t compare a quote for immediate retirement with another for retirement years later and attribute the difference to survivor coverage.

Here is a made-up 2026 illustration, not a plan quotation or a recommended division. Suppose a pension’s single-life form would pay the employee $2,400 a month. Suppose a form including survivor protection would instead pay $2,160 a month, with the same starting date. Those are assumed inputs. The plan, not this arithmetic, determines its actual quotes and survivor terms.

The difference in the total monthly pension is $2,400 minus $2,160 = $240. Across a full year of payments, $240 multiplied by 12 = $2,880. That tells you the difference in retirement payments under these assumed quotes. It does not value the survivor protection or say which form is better.

Now suppose the hypothetical agreement awards you 40 percent of each retirement payment under a shared payment arrangement. That percentage is another assumed input, not a state-law entitlement. Without survivor protection, your monthly share would be $2,400 multiplied by 0.40 = $960. With the quoted survivor form, it would be $2,160 multiplied by 0.40 = $864.

Your difference would be $960 minus $864 = $96 a month. Over a full payment year, $96 multiplied by 12 = $1,152. These are gross retirement amounts before taxes or other deductions. No survivor payment amount has been assumed. That requires the plan’s separate explanation of what is payable after death and what share, if any, your order assigns to you.

I would not dismiss the smaller quote merely because it is smaller. I also would not buy protection I hadn’t understood. Ask who bears any reduction and how the order expresses that allocation; our illustration simply assumes the retirement payment is reduced before your percentage is applied. Your arrangement could be different.

An election already made changes the conversation

Find out whether retirement payments have actually begun. A stated retirement intention, a signed election and a first payment are not interchangeable facts. Ask for the annuity starting date, the elected payment form, any survivor designation and any signed waiver or consent. Counsel can request records you cannot lawfully obtain yourself.

PBGC’s April 2026 drafting guidance says that after the participant has elected a benefit form and begun receiving payments, the named beneficiary and survivor benefits cannot be changed. That is a specific warning for PBGC-trusteed pensions, not a blanket description of every employer or government plan. It shows why “we’ll fix it after the divorce” can be a dangerous negotiating assumption.

If payments have begun, don’t decide from that warning that you have no rights. Existing rights, available divisions and remedies require an examination of the election, the plan and governing law. Call your divorce attorney, and ask whether a pension-order specialist is needed. If retirement is imminent, tell counsel the actual date rather than saying it is coming “soon.”

Pay for that help before signing: an award can omit death protection or use an unavailable payment form. Your attorney handles the legal entitlement; a specialist can help draft pension provisions the administrator can implement. A phone representative’s explanation does not settle the legal question.

If someone asks you to sign a survivor waiver, take the entire document to counsel before acting. Ask what payment would be surrendered, who would receive it instead, and whether the choice can later be changed. You need an answer tied to your papers, not an assurance that waivers are standard.

The Social Security question Bonnie raised

Bonnie, my choir friend, pointed out that a divorced-spouse Social Security benefit might be available without reducing Russ’s own benefit. I had assumed one person’s check had to come out of the other’s; SSA’s guidance says it doesn’t. Under SSA’s rules checked in October 2026, the retirement route generally requires a marriage lasting at least ten years, a finally divorced claimant who is unmarried and at least 62, and an application. SSA checks the worker’s insured status, age and benefit entitlement, and compares the claimant’s own-record entitlement with the divorced-spouse benefit; a higher own-record entitlement can mean no additional divorced-spouse payment. If the worker is already entitled to retirement or disability benefits, the two-year divorce wait is not a general requirement. If the worker has not filed, the independent route requires a fully insured worker at least 62 and at least two continuous years of final divorce, along with the claimant’s other requirements. Confirm your exact dates and eligibility at SSA’s family eligibility page; its detailed rules are in POMS RS 00202.005. For claiming-age decisions, use Social Security, Claimed On Purpose, the companion 2027 guide. This is a separate federal benefit question, not a pension share your attorney can bargain into the settlement.

Five pension questions before you sign

Put the pension’s full legal name at the top of a sheet, with the administrator’s contact and the date of the estimate you’re using. Then take these five questions to your attorney. Ask which answers require written confirmation from the administrator.

  1. What exactly am I being awarded or giving up? Identify the state-law retirement interest, any survivor rights, the calculation dates and the pension order provisions that carry out the agreement.
  2. Which payment arrangement can this plan implement now? Ask whether payments have begun, whether shared payment or separate interest is available, and what determines your starting date and payment duration.
  3. What would I receive if the employee dies before retirement payments start, and after they start? Have both situations answered, with the assigned survivor amount or method, eligibility conditions and any existing competing rights identified.
  4. What are the written estimates for the available payment forms? Require matching starting-date and service assumptions, and an explanation of any reduction, who bears it, and whether the amounts are gross or net.
  5. What must be done before the decree, an election or a waiver to preserve the intended rights? Record the actual deadlines, who drafts and submits the necessary order, and how you will obtain confirmation of the pension and survivor provisions accepted by the plan.

Leave room under each question for the answer and the document that supports it. “Asked” is not the same as “answered.” If the response refers to a plan section, keep that section with the estimate. If it says an option is unavailable, have counsel explain what that does to the proposed agreement before you accept a substitute.

Before your next signing appointment, put the retirement estimate and the survivor provisions beside the draft decree. Mark the place that answers what happens after a death. If you can’t find it, that is the question to bring through the door.

Chapter 13: The House Has a Yearly Price

The air conditioner stopped in July. I stood under the kitchen vent with my hand raised, waiting for something cooler than the room to come out. Nothing did. The replacement cost me $4,180 in 2020. Later came the roof.

I had kept the family house in Gilbert. The draft in Chapter 11 had left it with Russ; that changed before the final settlement. I wanted to stay where I knew the light switches and where my piano fit. In 2019, those seemed like solid reasons. They weren’t a budget.

Two years after the divorce, I sold. The patio home I bought in Mesa in 2021 suited the life I was living. Those repair bills hadn’t proved that owning a house was foolish. They had proved that I hadn’t priced this one properly.

You can love a house and still need to sell it. You can also keep it, provided the numbers support keeping it. I don’t want to talk you out of your kitchen. I want you to know what it asks of you after everyone else has left.

Separate the address from the offer

Write down what staying would preserve: proximity to work, a room you use to earn income, neighbors you can call, space for family. These benefits belong in a financial discussion.

Ask which benefits require this particular house. A familiar neighborhood may be available from a smaller rental nearby. A piano needs a room, but not necessarily its old room. Moving farther away might create transportation costs or take you away from help. Put those differences into the comparison.

The wrong advice here is that you must keep the house for stability. Stability that depends on ignoring an insurance renewal is fragile. The opposite advice, that you must sell because you’re single now, is no better. A paid-off house with manageable costs and suitable space can make sense. Paid off does not mean free to occupy.

The legal share is a separate question. State law varies on property division, separate contributions and what a court can order. California Courts’ Property and debts in a divorce, for example, distinguishes community, separate and mixed property interests. A house bought with funds from different sources may need more examination than its address and current value suggest.

That California guidance isn’t the rule for every state, and my Arizona settlement isn’t yours. Using the title and acquisition records from Chapter 10, have your attorney identify your state’s official court guidance or statute and determine what interest is being divided. Don’t turn an equal-share illustration below into your own legal entitlement.

Include what you would give up elsewhere in the settlement. The pension valuation caution from Chapter 12 applies even when the proposed exchange is a house.

Build the year, not the mortgage payment

Start with costs under the proposed arrangement. If keeping the house requires a new mortgage, the old payment is not your number. If you will hire someone for work your spouse used to do, price that work too.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau explains the distinction between principal and interest and the total mortgage payment. Your lender’s total can include mortgage insurance and an escrow payment for property taxes and homeowners insurance. Association dues may be separate.

Read the statement’s breakdown. For the worksheet below, put principal and interest on the first line, taxes and property coverage on their own lines, and any mortgage insurance with financing rather than property coverage. If you start with the full payment that already includes escrow and add the tax and insurance bills again, you have counted the same costs twice.

For taxes, obtain the current bill from the local taxing authority and ask whether a change of ownership or household status affects your assessment or any exemption. For insurance, request a quote for the proposed ownership and occupancy. Don’t assume the old policy or premium follows you unchanged. Ask what coverage and deductibles would apply, including any separate coverage your property needs.

Use a full year of utility bills rather than the comfortable month you remember. Check association notices for assessments already announced. Price the routine work you won’t do yourself, from cleaning gutters to servicing equipment.

There is no national repair allowance here. Ask qualified tradespeople about the roof and equipment and obtain written estimates for approaching work. A percentage of the house’s value can’t tell you whether your air conditioner will survive the summer. Treat uncertainty as a reason to keep cash available, not as permission to enter zero.

The true cost of keeping the house

Put the property address, estimate date and budget year at the top of a sheet. These five lines are a cash-funding plan, not a tax worksheet or a calculation of investment return. Beside each amount, note the bill or quote that supports it and anything still unconfirmed.

  1. Financing for the year. Proposed monthly principal and interest multiplied by 12, plus mortgage insurance if applicable. Use zero for principal and interest only if no loan will remain or be needed for the settlement.
  2. Property taxes. The annual amount expected under your proposed ownership, checked with the taxing authority; don’t add it again through escrow.
  3. Property coverage. Annual premiums for the coverage you need. Note the deductible separately as a possible cash demand, not a premium already paid.
  4. Running the property. Utilities, association dues and known assessments, plus routine maintenance or services you will pay for. Keep the component amounts beside the combined line.
  5. Repairs and replacements. Cash you need to set aside this year for identified work and uncertain failures. Show any urgent bill and your starting repair cash beside this line. Money already reserved is not another year’s expense.

Add the annual amounts, then divide by 12 for a monthly funding equivalent. Keep one-time buyout and refinancing cash outside that total.

Here is an invented 2026 example. None of these inputs is a national price, a lender quote or my repair history. Assume principal and interest of $1,350 a month, with no mortgage insurance. The annual financing line is $1,350 multiplied by 12 = $16,200.

Assume annual property taxes of $3,600 and property coverage of $1,800. Running costs are $3,300 for utilities, $600 for association dues and $1,500 for routine maintenance: $3,300 + $600 + $1,500 = $5,400. There are no additional known assessments in this example. Assume another $4,000 will be set aside for repairs and replacements.

The full-year funding total is $16,200 + $3,600 + $1,800 + $5,400 + $4,000 = $31,000. Dividing $31,000 by 12 gives about $2,583.33 a month, rounded to cents. That is the housing amount to carry into Chapter 20, not the assumed principal-and-interest payment.

Some principal repayment builds equity, and money reserved for repairs may remain unspent, but both require cash in this funding plan that you can’t also use for groceries. This total excludes your other living expenses and any one-time settlement costs.

An annual allowance does not answer whether you can pay a bill tomorrow. In a separate stress test for this 2026 example, suppose you start with $6,000 of repair cash and face an immediate $12,000 roof invoice. The gap is $12,000 minus $6,000 = $6,000. Future monthly savings do not fill it today.

If that repair will actually be paid this year, revise the repair line and the timing of the cash. Don’t count both the full invoice and a reserve intended to pay that same invoice. Leave any funding for other possible failures separately identified. A worksheet that works only when everything happens in December needs another pass.

A buyout can change the loan completely

Keeping the house may require compensating your spouse for an agreed interest. Identify where that money comes from. Cash paid to your spouse won’t be available for the first repair.

Use a separate invented 2026 property example. Assume an agreed value of $480,000 and a mortgage payoff of $180,000. Gross equity is $480,000 minus $180,000 = $300,000. That is a starting balance-sheet figure, not sale proceeds and not a finding that you each own half.

Suppose this keep-house proposal calls for a $150,000 cash buyout. That amount is an assumption about the agreement. If you need to borrow the entire buyout and refinance the old mortgage, $180,000 + $150,000 = $330,000 is needed before loan costs.

If another $6,000 of loan fees would be financed, the proposed new principal becomes $330,000 + $6,000 = $336,000. Financing those fees is itself subject to lender acceptance. Prepaid items or initial escrow funding may create additional cash needs; have the lender show where each amount is paid.

That loan is unrelated to the worksheet’s assumed $1,350 payment. Obtain its actual terms and rebuild the financing line; the balance, rate and repayment period determine the new commitment.

Freddie Mac’s Planning to refinance explains that a refinance replaces your current mortgage with a new loan. For a proposal that removes your ex through refinancing, have the lender confirm who will borrow on the replacement loan and how the existing loan will be paid off. Have counsel and the closing professional coordinate the deed and buyout with the financing. Don’t transfer an ownership interest on the strength of a casual promise that the loan will be handled later.

You can also ask the existing servicer whether this particular loan permits an assumption and an express release of the departing borrower, without assuming either is available or a title transfer accomplishes both. Chapter 14 handles the remaining debt-liability question; here, the point is whether a workable financing arrangement exists for keeping the house.

A quote is not approval

Before agreeing to a refinance deadline you haven’t tested, explain the proposed settlement to lenders and ask which income records and property documents they will need to evaluate it. Ask how they would evaluate support payments or retirement income you expect to use, rather than treating either as automatically acceptable.

The CFPB says debt-to-income limits differ across loan products and lenders. There is no single qualification percentage here. And qualification isn’t comfort: the lender’s review doesn’t build your allowance for replacing appliances or paying for health coverage.

For a refinance covered by the standard disclosures, ask for a Loan Estimate. The CFPB’s Loan Estimate Explainer shows the loan amount and term, projected payments, estimated closing costs and estimated cash to close. Compare offers on matching borrowing amounts and terms, and ask what is included in each payment.

The CFPB also states that receiving a Loan Estimate does not mean your application has been approved or denied, so ask what conditions remain before closing and when a rate lock expires. A friendly conversation is not evidence that your buyout money will be ready on the date in the agreement.

Read the repayment period alongside the payment. Freddie Mac warns that extending a mortgage’s term can increase total interest paid. Ask for a comparison over your intended holding period, including fees and remaining balances. A lower payment produced by more years of borrowing has bought breathing room; it hasn’t necessarily bought a cheaper house.

If neither spouse can qualify for the required financing alone, a promise to try again later isn’t a completed solution. Ask your attorney about a sale or another legally workable arrangement. If temporary shared ownership is proposed, counsel should address payment responsibilities, occupancy, repairs and a definite exit mechanism. Don’t assume a court will approve your preferred terms.

Call your divorce attorney before signing the house provision, especially if qualification is uncertain or either of you refuses to cooperate, because counsel needs to address the legal consequence if financing fails. Ask a CPA to review a proposed sale or asset exchange before you commit, so the comparison includes tax consequences rather than only cash at closing.

Sale proceeds aren’t the number on the listing

Ask the real estate professional or closing agent for a written seller net estimate at a defensible price. It should account for loan payoffs and all expected selling charges, including agreed compensation, fees and any buyer credits. Use actual terms, not an assumed universal commission rate.

Return to the separate 2026 property example: $480,000 value, $180,000 payoff. Suppose a sale actually closes at $480,000 and total selling charges and credits are $30,000. The cash before income tax is $480,000 minus $180,000 minus $30,000 = $270,000.

If this hypothetical agreement divides that net amount equally, each share is $270,000 divided by 2 = $135,000. The equal division is assumed, not prescribed by state law. This sale calculation also doesn’t establish what costs a keep-house buyout must deduct; that’s a separate negotiating and legal question.

That $270,000 is a proceeds calculation, not a calculation of taxable gain. IRS Publication 523, Selling Your Home, explains the tax rules; Chapter 17 covers them. Have your CPA examine the proposed sale dates before you count the entire share as spendable.

Replacement housing needs its own estimate. Still within this invented 2026 example, suppose your $135,000 share must cover $5,000 of moving and temporary housing and $45,000 of down payment and purchase costs for a replacement home. That leaves $135,000 minus $5,000 minus $45,000 = $85,000 before any income-tax reserve or other settlement obligations.

Renting instead may preserve more cash initially, but deposits, moving expenses and monthly rent still belong in the comparison. Obtain real quotes for the places you could actually live. Compare their full housing costs with the five-line total, not rent with principal and interest alone.

Give waiting a price and an end date

Ask a local real estate professional for recent comparable closed sales and a realistic price range, accounting for the property’s condition. An online estimate is a starting question, not an agreed valuation. Neither tells you what a future buyer will pay.

If waiting is proposed, price the delay. Identify the additional interest, taxes, insurance and upkeep, any overlapping housing cost, and work needed before listing. Distinguish those costs from principal repayment and repair money that merely stays reserved. Don’t subtract the entire cash-funding worksheet from a hoped-for price increase as though every dollar were an expense.

Then have counsel connect the plan to the decree or settlement. Ask who chooses the agent, who approves a price reduction, who pays carrying costs, and how necessary repairs are authorized. Ask what happens if one person won’t sign or if a refinance attempt fails. Those are drafting questions under your state’s law, not instructions to impose a private deadline yourself.

If the sale will happen after the divorce, ask how the agreement covers occupancy and the route to closing. If it will happen before, ask what permissions or existing orders govern the listing and use of proceeds. Give the proposed dates to your CPA too, because moving the sale across the decree date is a decision to review with your own records, not a tax shortcut to assume.

Don’t postpone a call about a court deadline or threatened missed payment while trying to find the perfect selling season. My preference is for a bounded plan with a fallback, not a plan that depends on a better market arriving before the next bill.

Before the next settlement meeting, write the yearly housing total beside the proposed cash buyout and the cash left afterward. Put the unanswered lender question underneath. Take that sheet with you, even if you still want the house.

Chapter 14: Equal Balances, Unequal Money

Two statements sit beside a proposed agreement. One shows cash. The other shows shares bought years ago. The totals match, and someone has drawn a neat line between them: one account for each spouse.

Your calculator agrees. You put it down.

Pick it up again after you find the purchase records. Equal balances can carry different future tax bills. And the credit card assigned to your ex on the next page may still have your name on the lender’s contract. Both differences belong in the discussion before you sign.

The paper division can leave you with less spendable money and a debt the lender still expects you to pay. You don’t have to become an accountant to notice. You need a sheet that keeps the missing information visible.

Put the whole offer on one dated sheet

Use the inventory from Chapter 10 rather than starting another search. This time, bring the assets and debts together so you can examine a proposed division. A marital balance sheet is a working record of what might be divided, not a declaration that every item on it legally belongs to both of you.

Put disputed ownership on the sheet too. Label it disputed. State law varies on separate property, mixed contributions, valuation dates and responsibility for debts. The state-law classification caution from Chapter 13 applies to the other assets as well. Ask counsel which local statute or official court instructions govern, and have the disputed entries reviewed against those rules. An account’s title alone isn’t the analysis.

Choose a common comparison date with your attorney, then show the actual statement date beside each figure. If an investment statement is old, don’t quietly compare it with today’s loan balance. Ask for an updated value. Keep the agreed legal valuation date distinct from the date you are checking whether the proposal still works financially.

For a taxable brokerage account, request the holdings and adjusted basis, not just its total. For a car, list its defensible current value and its loan separately. For household property, distinguish a possible resale price from what you paid to buy it. A receipt for a new dining table doesn’t show what someone would pay for the used one.

Record retirement assets by tax category, using the work from Chapters 11 and 12: tax-deferred, Roth with conditions to check, or another category the CPA identifies. Bring the house result from Chapter 13. Examine the entire exchange, not just its most attractive item.

A missing basis or unresolved business value stays marked unknown, with a note naming the document needed and who will request it. A total with an unresolved value isn’t finished.

The old purchase price follows the shares

IRS Publication 504, Divorced or Separated Individuals, explains that property transfers between spouses, or between former spouses when incident to divorce, generally produce no recognized gain or loss. The same publication says the recipient takes the transferor’s adjusted basis. The edition available when checked in October 2026 is for 2025 returns, not a published 2026-return edition.

IRS Publication 550’s Stocks and Bonds section explains that basis for purchased shares generally begins with purchase price and purchase costs, then changes for specified events. The resulting adjusted basis is used to determine gain or loss on sale. It isn’t today’s statement balance.

The divorce transfer does not generally reset that basis to market value. If your spouse transfers appreciated shares to you in a qualifying transfer, you receive their existing tax history along with the shares. A later sale can realize the appreciation that accumulated before you owned them individually.

“No recognized gain on the transfer” is not a promise about tax on the eventual sale.

Have your CPA confirm that the proposed transfer qualifies as incident to divorce. Publication 504 sets timing and relationship-to-divorce requirements and lists exceptions, including a transfer to a nonresident alien spouse, certain trust transfers and certain stock redemptions. A delayed transfer or an unusual arrangement needs review, not a casual assumption that any payment connected with an ex is covered.

Also distinguish moving shares from selling them and moving the cash. Publication 504 separately addresses sales of jointly owned property: recognized gain or loss must be reported, with each spouse’s share determined under the applicable state ownership law. Ask the CPA who would report a proposed sale before anyone presses the sell button.

What two matching totals can conceal

Here is an invented 2026 comparison. It is not a recommended division, a market forecast or a calculation of your tax. Assume one taxable brokerage account contains shares worth $100,000, with verified adjusted basis of $20,000. Another holds $100,000 of cash. Ignore accrued interest, trading costs and price changes for this illustration.

If the shares transfer to you under the general divorce-transfer rule, their assumed basis remains $20,000. If you then sell all of them for $100,000, the assumed gain is $100,000 minus $20,000 = $80,000. The full sale proceeds are not the taxable gain.

For arithmetic only, assume tax equal to 15 percent of the gain. That isn’t a 2026 federal or state rate for your situation. Your income, holding period and other tax facts require a CPA’s calculation.

The assumed tax is $80,000 multiplied by 0.15 = $12,000. After setting aside that amount, the assumed sale proceeds available are $100,000 minus $12,000 = $88,000. Under these deliberately limited assumptions, receiving the other account’s existing cash gives $100,000 without a sale of appreciated shares.

The difference is $100,000 minus $88,000 = $12,000, despite matching statement totals. That is the assumed sale-tax cost, not a tax caused by the qualifying divorce transfer.

You might keep the shares. Future prices and your actual taxes could change the result. Ask for both the property value and the cash available under your intended sale plan; don’t deduct our invented percentage from every offer.

If you need living money immediately, an offer made entirely of investments is not the same practical offer as cash already available. Tell the CPA when you expect to sell and how much you need. Tell counsel which estimates are conditional, rather than presenting an estimated future tax as an established settlement deduction.

Nor does this example tell you how to trade taxable shares against a tax-deferred retirement account. That comparison needs the actual account’s tax character and intended withdrawal schedule. Have a CPA examine it before signing; the transfer mechanics from Chapter 11 don’t make different dollars interchangeable.

Get the records for the shares you will receive

A brokerage account can contain many purchases of the same security. Each purchase group is a tax lot. Publication 550 addresses identifying the particular shares sold or transferred. Ask which lots you will receive and how their basis and acquisition dates will be recorded.

Publication 504 requires the transferring spouse to provide enough records to determine adjusted basis and holding period at the transfer date. Have counsel address delivery of those records. Request them before negotiating around a basis figure.

If a statement shows no basis, don’t substitute current value or zero. Give the CPA purchase and transfer records you can lawfully obtain; counsel can request missing history through disclosure.

Ask the receiving brokerage how it will confirm the holdings and basis after transfer. Save its confirmation with the source records. If the entries don’t match, raise the discrepancy before a planned sale. Your document folder should explain the number, not merely contain a screenshot of it.

If the proposed holdings are concentrated in one company, flag that alongside the tax estimate. Ask a qualified adviser about the investment risk and a CPA about the cost of changing the holdings. Don’t accept a familiar company name as a substitute for examining what would happen to your spending plan if its price fell.

Stop at the business interest or the stock award

Restricted stock, stock units, options and deferred compensation need their actual award documents. An employer portal’s headline value doesn’t answer when a benefit becomes available, whether it can be transferred, what conditions could prevent payment or who will owe tax. Ask counsel to obtain the grant agreements and applicable plan terms.

Publication 504’s property-transfer guidance specifically distinguishes income treatment for nonstatutory stock options and nonqualified deferred compensation. That is a warning against treating every employment award as ordinary purchased shares, not permission to apply one tax result to every award with stock in its name.

Have your attorney bring in a valuation professional experienced with the asset and a CPA before you accept an exchange involving these benefits. They need to identify the divisible interest under your state law, price what is actually available and establish the tax treatment. You can gather the papers. Don’t supply the missing valuation yourself.

The same boundary applies to a closely held business: a company interest without a ready public market. A percentage of ownership is not a price. The company’s bank balance isn’t a value you can multiply by that percentage, and annual revenue isn’t cash the owner can withdraw.

Give the professionals the ownership agreements, financial statements, tax returns and relevant debt records. Ask which restrictions, valuation date and ownership rights their analysis uses. If someone proposes that your ex keep the business while paying you later, have counsel examine that payment promise separately from the business value. An installment you hope to receive is not money already in your account.

Record any personal guaranty — your promise to answer for a business debt — as potential exposure, not automatically an extra debt to subtract. Ask counsel whether it remains enforceable and what would release it. Receiving no business ownership doesn’t establish release.

Match every debt to its contract

The Federal Trade Commission’s How To Get Out of Debt distinguishes unsecured debts, such as ordinary credit card balances, from debts secured by collateral, such as a house or car. Collateral is property supporting the lender’s claim. With secured debt, ask counsel what rights the lender has against that property as well as against the borrowers.

An unsecured card isn’t harmless because no car is attached to it. A secured car loan isn’t solved because your ex will drive the car. Record the people on the borrowing agreement separately from the people on the title and the person receiving the asset.

In a separate invented 2026 example, suppose a car is worth $24,000 and the loan payoff is $29,000. Its net position is $24,000 minus $29,000 = negative $5,000. Awarding the car doesn’t produce $24,000 of debt-free property. Ask the lender and counsel how the loan would be addressed, including any shortfall in a proposed sale.

Use gross values with separate debts, or clearly identified net values. Listing the car at $24,000 and subtracting its $29,000 loan already gives negative $5,000; don’t enter that net figure again. If a professional uses net values, ask which debts are included.

The distinction between your decree and your lender agreement is the hard part. A decree assigns responsibility between spouses; it is not itself a lender’s release of someone who signed its contract. California Courts’ Common challenges when splitting debt gives a concrete example: a creditor need not honor the spouses’ payment agreement, and missed payments on joint debt may affect both borrowers’ credit.

That guidance is a verified California example, not a determination of your personal liability. State law and the contract matter. Put this question to your attorney for every lingering debt: “Under this agreement and my state’s law, can the lender still demand payment from me after the divorce?” Ask the creditor to confirm your recorded borrower status and what documents would change it.

Don’t infer your status from possession of a card. Joint borrowers, cosigners and authorized users are different categories to investigate. Ask the issuer which you are, then have counsel assess your exposure. Debt in only your spouse’s name also belongs in the legal review if state marital-debt rules could affect you; a missing signature isn’t a universal answer either.

The mortgage from Chapter 13 needs this contract check too. Don’t treat a deed changing ownership as a borrower release; give counsel the loan documents and the servicer’s written answer.

Count a release only when it is completed

Discuss payoff, refinancing into the responsible person’s name or a formal creditor-approved release with counsel and the lender. Availability depends on the account and approval. Each proposed route needs evidence that it happened, not merely an obligation in the decree to try.

For payoff, obtain the lender’s current payoff instructions and confirmation afterward. For refinancing, confirm that the replacement borrowing actually paid off the old joint obligation. For a formal release, get the creditor’s written release and have counsel check whether it covers the existing balance as well as future borrowing.

Closing a card to new charges and removing liability for its existing debt are separate questions. Ask the issuer about both. A replacement card number, a changed mailing address or removal from online access isn’t the document proving release.

If a joint debt must remain temporarily, have your attorney address who pays, how you receive lawful payment confirmations and what happens at a missed payment or failed refinance. Ask about enforceable reimbursement provisions and remedies in your state. They may protect rights between the two of you; don’t describe them as protection that automatically stops a creditor.

Get the payment date and monitoring arrangement into the written plan. Your ex’s promise may be sincere. It still isn’t a creditor’s release.

If your ex misses the assigned card payment

Keep the creditor problem and the family-court problem separate. You may need to address both.
