California’s court guide warns that going back to family court about an ex’s payment agreement may not fix credit reporting or stop creditor calls. Ask your own attorney what enforcement is available; don’t assume that example supplies your state’s procedure.

Use this response sequence for a joint account still connected to you:

  1. Confirm the facts through the creditor’s official contact. Use your statement or the institution’s verified site. Ask about the balance, payment status, due date and your borrower status. Save the statement and call notes.
  2. Send the notice and relevant decree provision to counsel promptly. Ask about your contractual exposure, available enforcement and whether an immediate payment is appropriate. Do not ignore a court notice while waiting for an answer from your ex. If the next payment is due before counsel can answer and you are responsible under the creditor agreement, ask counsel urgently and arrange an on-time payment you can afford; keep proof and pursue any reimbursement separately. If you dispute liability, ask counsel before acknowledging or paying a possibly time-barred debt.
  3. If payment is needed but you cannot afford it, contact the creditor about available arrangements. The FTC advises contacting creditors rather than waiting for collection. Obtain any proposed terms in writing and discuss them with counsel before accepting new liability.
  4. Check credit reporting and preserve the evidence. The CFPB’s How do I dispute an error on my credit report? directs consumers to contact both the reporting company and the company supplying the information when an error appears. Identify the actual error and keep supporting copies.

An accurate missed payment doesn’t become inaccurate because your ex violated the decree. Don’t file a false dispute claiming the debt was never yours. If responsibility is genuinely disputed, have counsel help you state the facts; if you pay to protect yourself, preserve proof and ask about reimbursement without assuming you will recover it.

The one-page balance sheet

Write the comparison date and proposal date at the top, with supporting records behind the sheet. Continue on another page if needed. Leave unknowns visible.

  • For each asset: description and institution, market value and date, adjusted basis if known, named owner or title, tax character, proposed recipient and any disputed legal interest. Mark business or pension valuations requiring professional work.
  • For each debt: creditor, balance and date, secured or unsecured status, collateral if any, names and roles on the contract, assigned payer under the proposal or decree, and the attorney’s answer about continuing lender rights.
  • For each unfinished transfer or release: action required, person responsible, deadline, evidence still needed and where the completed confirmation will be saved. Keep estimated sale taxes and costs separate from current debt balances.

Add asset values and subtract debts counted only once. Label that result a current balance-sheet total before estimated taxes and transaction costs, not the money you can spend. Beside your proposed share, identify what is available now, what needs a sale and what depends on someone completing paperwork or making later payments.

Before the next meeting, circle one unknown basis and every debt that would remain tied to you. Put the CPA’s name beside the first and your attorney’s beside the debts. Leave the circles there until an answer arrives.

Chapter 15: A Number, a Date, and What It’s Worth After Tax

Somewhere in the draft there is a paragraph with a dollar amount and a number of months in it. Support. One line, after pages about the house and the accounts.

The first question most people ask about that line is whether the amount is enough, or too much. Fair question. It isn’t the first one.

Ask instead what the payment is worth after tax, who decides whether it continues, and what makes it stop. Those three answers can move the real number more than another round of arguing about the amount.

The word your state uses may not be the word the IRS uses

Your court papers may say spousal support, maintenance, or spousal maintenance. California’s self-help guide, for example, calls it spousal support and notes the term alimony means the same thing there. Which word appears in your order is a matter of your state’s law and your court’s forms.

Federal tax law uses alimony or separate maintenance. The two vocabularies do not always line up, and a payment called support in a state order is not automatically alimony for federal tax purposes.

IRS Topic 452 lists what has to be true for a payment to be alimony or separate maintenance federally. The spouses don’t file a joint return with each other. The payment is in cash, including checks and money orders. It is made to or for a spouse or former spouse under a divorce or separation instrument. If the spouses are legally separated under a decree of divorce or separate maintenance, they aren’t members of the same household when the payment is made. There is no liability to make a payment, in cash or property, after the recipient spouse’s death. The payment isn’t treated as child support or a property settlement. And the instrument doesn’t designate the payment as not alimony.

That last requirement surprises people. Under Publication 504, spouses can include a provision stating that otherwise qualifying payments aren’t alimony, and a recipient who excludes them has to attach a copy of that designation to their return each year it applies. The document can decide the characterization.

Use that list to mark questions, not to classify the payment yourself. Have your family-law attorney and CPA review the actual proposed instrument together before you sign; the heading on the form does not settle the federal treatment.

What it isn’t

Child support is a different thing with different rules. The IRS says plainly that child support is never deductible and isn’t considered income to the person receiving it. Publication 504 adds a trap worth knowing if your instrument predates 2019 and calls for both: when the payer pays less than the total required, the payments apply to child support first, and only the remainder is treated as alimony.

A property settlement is also a different thing. Chapter 14 covered the transfer side of that, where a qualifying divorce transfer generally produces no recognized gain or loss and carries the old basis along with it. Support is a stream of payments. Property division is a one-time allocation of what you already own together. They trade against each other at the negotiating table, and they are not the same asset.

Topic 452 lists several payments that are not alimony even when they appear in a divorce file. Child support. Noncash property settlements, lump sum or installments. Payments that are a spouse’s part of community property income. Payments to keep up the payer’s own property, or the use of that property. And voluntary payments, meaning payments not required by an instrument.

Voluntary is the one I’d underline. Money handed over because it seemed decent, outside any order or written agreement, doesn’t get alimony treatment, and depending on your state and your order it may not count toward anything either. If you intend a payment to have legal effect, it belongs in a document.

Who decides, and on what

There is no national alimony formula. Whether support is awarded, how much, for how long, and whether it can be changed later are questions of the law of the state that governs your case and of the terms your order ends up containing.

I know how unsatisfying that is when you want a number. I’d rather give you an unsatisfying truth than a tidy answer that doesn’t govern your case.

California publishes a useful example of what the inside of that decision looks like. Its courts’ guide distinguishes temporary support, ordered while the case is pending, from long-term support ordered at the end of the case. It also says many marriages and domestic partnerships end without either spouse paying long-term support.

For long-term support, that guide says there is no math formula. The judge must weigh a list of statutory factors. Length of the marriage. Each person’s age and health. Incomes, and earning capacity including the time and cost of gaining skills. The marital standard of living. The property and debt each person has. Whether one spouse helped the other get an education or a license. Need and ability to pay. The impact of tax law on support. Any history of abuse during the marriage.

On duration, the same guide states an assumption for shorter marriages: support will last half the length of the marriage. For marriages longer than ten years it says there is no such assumption. Support may then last as long as one spouse needs it and the other can pay.

That is California’s framework. It is not the rule where you live, and I am not offering it as a prediction for you. I’m offering it because it shows the shape of the question: a list of factors, a judge with discretion, and no arithmetic that produces the answer.

So get the framework that actually governs you. Ask counsel whether the governing jurisdiction uses a guideline calculation, a factor-based discretionary standard, or different approaches for temporary and long-term support. Ask where that rule is published. Then ask what the orders in your court have looked like for situations resembling yours, understanding that an answer about the past is not a promise.

The honest headline here is that a long marriage does not entitle you to long support everywhere, and a comfortable marital standard of living is no assurance that it will be maintained. Two households cost more to run than one did. Chapter 20 does that arithmetic without comfort.

The date on the instrument changes the tax

This is the part where a reader can save or lose real money by understanding one date.

For divorce or separation instruments executed after December 31, 2018, Publication 504 says the payer gets no deduction for alimony and the recipient leaves it out of gross income. For instruments executed on or before that date, the older treatment still applies: deductible by the payer, reportable as income by the recipient.

A pre-2019 instrument can be pulled into the new treatment, but only in a specific way. Publication 504 says the post-2018 rules apply to alimony under an instrument executed before 2019 and modified after 2018 if the modification expressly states that the alimony isn’t deductible to the payer or includible in the recipient’s income. A modification that merely changes the amount doesn’t do it. The publication’s own example describes a 2016 decree modified in 2025 to increase the monthly payment, where the modification said nothing about the repeal, and the result is that all the payments made that year stayed deductible and taxable under the old rules.

The timing can also split a single year. In another Publication 504 example, where the modification does expressly adopt the new rules partway through the year, payments before the change keep the old treatment and payments after it get the new one.

And the operative date is the date of the instrument the payments are actually made under. Publication 504 describes a written separation agreement executed in October 2018 that, under the law of that state, survived the divorce as an independent contract and was deliberately not merged into the later decree. Payments under that agreement kept the old treatment even though the divorce decree was executed in 2025. In a different example, where the decree itself awarded the support after 2018, the new rules applied to payments made under the decree.

Three practical consequences. First, if you are negotiating now, your instrument will almost certainly be a post-2018 one, so plan on the payment being neither deductible nor taxable federally, and confirm that with your CPA rather than with a decade-old article. Second, if you have an older order and someone proposes modifying it, the exact words of the modification are a tax decision, not just a legal one, and your CPA should see the language before it is signed. Third, state income tax is its own question. Ask your CPA how your state treats these payments, because federal treatment doesn’t settle it.

One more detail for anyone living under a pre-2019 order. Publication 504 notes that taxable alimony counts as compensation for IRA contribution and deduction limits, but only for instruments executed on or before December 31, 2018 that haven’t been modified to exclude those amounts. If you’re still receiving taxable alimony and want to contribute to an IRA, that’s a CPA question with a real answer. The same publication also describes a recapture rule that can apply when payments under a pre-2019 instrument drop sharply in the first three years. If your old order has declining payments, don’t guess at that one.

Run the number both ways before you argue about it

What follows is invented, dated 2026, and built only to show the arithmetic. The tax rates are assumptions rather than rates for your income, and I’ve used a single flat percentage where the real calculation works through brackets. Assume the payments qualify as alimony under the Internal Revenue Code and that no state income tax applies, which is a simplification, not a fact about your state.

Assume an order for $2,000 a month. The annual gross figure is $2,000 multiplied by 12 = $24,000.

Take the post-2018 instrument first. The recipient includes none of it in federal gross income, so federal income tax on the payment is zero and the cash kept for the year is $24,000. The payer takes no deduction, so the federal cost of the payment is the full $24,000.

Now take a pre-2019 instrument that was never modified. The recipient reports the $24,000 as income. Assume, for arithmetic only, a 12 percent rate: $24,000 multiplied by 0.12 = $2,880 of assumed tax, leaving $24,000 minus $2,880 = $21,120. The payer deducts the $24,000. A deduction reduces taxable income rather than paying a bill directly, so its value depends on the payer’s rate. Assume 22 percent for arithmetic: $24,000 multiplied by 0.22 = $5,280 of assumed tax reduction, making the net cost $24,000 minus $5,280 = $18,720.

Same $24,000 on the page. Under these assumptions the recipient’s spendable amount differs by $24,000 minus $21,120 = $2,880, and the payer’s cost differs by $24,000 minus $18,720 = $5,280.

Run it backwards too, because that is how the negotiation actually works. If the goal under the old rules were to leave the recipient with $24,000 after the assumed 12 percent tax, the gross needed would be $24,000 divided by 0.88, which is about $27,272.73. The after-tax target and the gross number are not the same number, and whichever one you forget is the one that will bite.

The estimate to build before your next meeting

Write it on one sheet, with the assumption behind every line.

  1. The execution date that governs. The date of the instrument the payments would be made under, and whether any proposed modification expressly adopts the post-2018 rules. If you don’t know, that is the first question for counsel and the CPA, not a blank to fill in with a guess.
  2. Gross support for a full year. The proposed monthly amount multiplied by the number of months payable in that year. Note separately any step-down or end date inside the year.
  3. Federal treatment under that date. Either not includible and not deductible, or includible and deductible. Write which one, and write that the CPA confirmed it.
  4. Assumed tax, labeled as an assumption. Your CPA’s estimated rate applied to the gross, plus a line for your state’s treatment. Keep the recipient’s figure and the payer’s figure separate; they are different calculations, not two sides of one.
  5. Net for the year, and when the cash arrives. Gross less assumed tax, then the payment dates. Money arriving monthly isn’t the same as money you have in March.

If you would receive taxable support under an older instrument, add a sixth line: estimated tax payments. Publication 504 notes that a person receiving alimony may have to make estimated tax payments, because nobody is withholding from it. A support check that feels adequate in May can feel very different in April if you’ve never set anything aside.

Take the sheet to the CPA before you take a position on the amount. An estimate built on the wrong execution date is worse than no estimate, because it feels like knowledge.

What ends it, and what can change it

Both of these are state-law questions, and the answers belong in the document rather than in your assumptions.

California’s guide again serves as an example of the kinds of endings an order can have: a written agreement about the ending date that the court signs off on, a court order ending it, the supported spouse’s remarriage, or the death of either spouse. For changes, the same guide says that if the parties can’t agree, the person asking must show a significant change in circumstances, and that a change in the amount can only reach back to the date the papers asking for the change were filed.

California makes the filing date important for its own modification rule. Ask your attorney whether your state uses a similar limit, and seek advice promptly when circumstances change.

Retirement deserves its own conversation in a late-life divorce. A support obligation that was affordable on a salary may not be affordable on a pension and Social Security, and whether retiring is a basis to change the order depends on your state’s law and on what the order says. Don’t assume turning 67 adjusts anything by itself. Ask before you sign, and ask again before you retire.

The recipient’s death, under federal tax law, is already in the picture: for a payment to be alimony there must be no liability to make payments after the recipient dies. What happens if the payer dies is a separate question, and it is one of the most commonly skipped items in a late-life settlement. Ask your attorney what happens to the support obligation then, whether your state allows security for it, and whether life insurance is appropriate and who would own and pay for the policy. Keep that question away from the beneficiary cleanup in Chapter 19, which is a different task with a different purpose.

Questions to take to a family-law attorney

Bring this written, the way Celia taught me to. You’ll get better answers, and a shorter bill, than you will from the version you improvise in the chair.

  1. Under the law that governs my case, is support decided by a guideline calculation, by a list of factors with judicial discretion, or by some combination, and is the rule different for temporary support than for long-term support? Where is it published?
  2. Which facts about my marriage and my finances matter most to that standard, and what documents should I bring to support them?
  3. Is support modifiable here, and on what showing? Can it be made non-modifiable by agreement, and what would that cost me or protect me from?
  4. What ends support under my state’s law and under this proposed language: an end date, remarriage, cohabitation, death, something else?
  5. If I remarry, or if my ex remarries, what changes?
  6. If either of us retires, does that support a change, and should the order say anything about it now?
  7. If the payer dies, what happens to the payments, and is security or insurance available and appropriate here?
  8. How does this support proposal interact with the property division we’re discussing, including the retirement accounts and the house?
  9. What is the enforcement route in my state if payments stop, and what does it realistically cost and take?
  10. What does the order need to say for my CPA to report this correctly, including the execution date and whether any modification adopts the post-2018 rules?

Number 8 is the one people skip, and in a divorce after fifty it may be the one that matters most. Support can end. A retirement account doesn’t stop existing in month sixty-one. If you are being asked to take more support and less of the retirement money, price both over the years you expect to live, with your attorney and a CPA, and not on the back of an envelope at the kitchen table at eleven at night.

Before you sign

Put the execution date, the federal treatment, the ending events and the modification standard in writing on one page, each with the name of the person who confirmed it. If a line has no name beside it, it isn’t confirmed; it’s a hope with a dollar sign in front of it.

Then read the support paragraph out loud. Slowly. If you can’t say what stops the payments and what the money is worth after tax, you’re not ready to sign that page yet, and nobody is entitled to rush you through it.

Chapter 16: Coverage Ends on a Date You Have to Ask For

The envelope came from a company I’d never heard of, which turned out to be the outfit Russ’s employer paid to run its benefits paperwork. Inside was an election notice with a monthly premium printed on it: $612.

I sat down with it and made the only comparison I had. Groceries were running about $340 a month for one person by then, and the utilities on the Gilbert house came to roughly $125 in a month when the air conditioner behaved. Add those: $340 + $125 = $465. The health insurance I’d carried for 31 years without ever once seeing its price was $612.

One plan, one employer, one year. It is not what yours will cost, and I’m not offering my premium as a benchmark for anybody. What it taught me is the part worth keeping: the price of my coverage had been invisible to me for three decades, and it became visible on a deadline.

The plan sets the date, not the courthouse

Your health coverage through a spouse’s employer plan does not end because a judge signed something. It ends under the terms of that plan, on a date the plan determines, and the people who know that date work for the plan.

Under federal law, divorce and legal separation are listed among the life events that can trigger continuation coverage rights. That is the formal name for keeping the same group plan temporarily at your own expense. Here is the horizon, stated the way the Department of Labor’s FAQs for workers state it. When divorce causes a former spouse to lose coverage under a covered plan, that spouse can generally elect up to 36 months of COBRA; 18 months is the usual period after job loss or reduced hours, subject to plan-specific conditions and early termination.

Here is the part that catches people, and it caught me. For a divorce or a legal separation that causes a loss of plan coverage, the duty to tell the plan administrator falls on the employee or the qualified beneficiary, not on the employer.

And there are two clocks, not one. People collapse them into a single deadline and then miss both.

The first is the notice clock, the one that runs to you telling the plan a divorce happened. For a private-sector plan under the Department of Labor’s rules, your deadline to give that notice cannot be less than 60 days from the latest of three dates. One, when the qualifying event takes place. Two, when the former spouse’s or child’s coverage runs out. Three, when official notice of your duty to inform the plan reaches you. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which administers the same statute for state and local government plans, describes that notice period as 60 days after the divorce, or after a legal separation that results in losing coverage.

The second is the election clock, the one that runs to you deciding whether to take the coverage. Under the Department of Labor’s guidance for private-sector plans, that period is at least 60 days measured from the later of the date coverage is lost or the date the election notice is given. Giving notice is not electing. Electing is a separate act, with a separate dated cutoff, and the plan will not treat your letter as both.

So write to the plan administrator now, before anything is final, and ask five things in writing. What date would my coverage under this plan end. What is the exact address, and in what form, for notice of a divorce or legal separation. What is my dated deadline for giving that notice. What is my dated deadline for electing coverage. What is the maximum continuation period for my situation and when does it start. Keep the reply. Request the current summary plan description and election materials; confirm the current notice address and dates in writing with the administrator. Whatever the two cutoffs turn out to be, act well before them rather than up against them.

CMS also takes the position, for the plans in its jurisdiction, that where a plan failed to properly inform a qualified beneficiary of that 60-day notice duty, the plan has to disregard the person’s failure to meet it. Don’t build a plan around that. Build a plan around writing the letter.

First, find out whether the law even reaches your plan

Not every employer plan is covered, and this is the question I’d put at the top of the page.

Federal COBRA applies to group health plans maintained by employers with 20 or more employees in the prior year. CMS, explaining the same statute, states that it does not apply to plans sponsored by the federal government, by the governments of the District of Columbia or any United States territory or possession, or by certain church-related organizations. Federal employees’ health benefits operate under a separate temporary continuation of coverage arrangement created by its own 1988 law.

If your spouse works for a small employer, the federal right may not be there at all. CMS points to state continuation coverage laws, sometimes called mini-COBRA, and says your state’s department of insurance can tell you whether your state requires that coverage. That is a phone call you make, not a thing you assume either way.

So the first line of any comparison is not a premium. It’s a sentence naming which law applies to this particular plan, and who told you so.

36 months does not reach 65

This is the arithmetic that changes how a fifty-something should think about continuation coverage, and almost nobody does it out loud.

I was 56 when my divorce was final. Medicare eligibility generally arrives at 65. That leaves 65 minus 56 = 9 years of coverage to arrange. A 36-month maximum is 3 years. So 9 minus 3 = 6 years that continuation coverage was never going to reach, no matter how diligently I filed anything.

Continuation coverage is a bridge. For a divorce in your fifties it is a bridge to another decision, not a bridge to Medicare. Plan the second decision while you still have the first one.

If you are nearing 65, ask the benefits administrator how your coverage ends and consult Medicare Made Plain, the 2027 enrollment guide in this same series, for Medicare enrollment and COBRA interactions.

One situation runs differently, and it’s common enough in a late-life divorce to name. Suppose your spouse’s job ended first and you were already on continuation coverage because of that. CMS describes a divorce occurring during that initial period as a second qualifying event, one that can extend a spouse’s maximum period to 36 months where the conditions are met and notice is given within 60 days. Same 60 days. Different starting clock. If that is your situation, ask the administrator in writing which period you are in and what the extension requires, because the answer depends on dates and not on what feels fair.

Note also what ends a continuation period early. CMS lists obtaining coverage under another employer’s group health plan after the election among them, which matters if you are weighing a job for its benefits. And the Department of Labor points out a related right: a spouse’s employer plan may allow special enrollment within 30 days of your loss of coverage, a shorter window than the Marketplace’s. If remarriage or a new job is anywhere in the picture, that 30-day figure is worth knowing before you need it.

Why the premium triples when nothing about the plan changes

Nothing about the coverage got more expensive. What ended was your spouse’s employer paying most of it.

CMS states the ceiling: premiums for continuation coverage cannot exceed 102 percent of the cost to the plan for similarly situated people who have not had a qualifying event. The cost to the plan means both the portion employees paid and the portion the employer paid, and the 2 percent is an administrative fee.

Made-up figures follow. Dated 2026, chosen to show the subtraction and nothing else. Assume a plan’s cost for similar coverage is $800 a month, of which the employee’s paycheck deduction covered $200 and the employer covered the other $600. The continuation premium can be up to $800 multiplied by 1.02 = $816 a month.

Compare that with the $200 that used to come out of a paycheck. The monthly increase is $816 minus $200 = $616. Across a year, $616 multiplied by 12 = $7,392 of household cost that was always there and was never visible on a pay stub.

Two payment mechanics matter more than they sound. CMS says the initial premium payment is due within 45 days after the date of the election, and later premiums are timely if paid by the due date or within a 30-day grace period. It also lists nonpayment among the reasons a continuation period ends early, along with the employer ceasing to maintain any group health plan.

Which brings up the settlement question. Your decree may say your ex pays the premium for a period. Ask your attorney what your state’s court can order and how it would be enforced, and understand that the distinction from Chapter 14 holds here too: an instruction between the two of you is not an arrangement with the plan. The plan bills the person who elected, and it can terminate the coverage for nonpayment. If someone else’s check is supposed to arrive, build in proof that it did, and a fallback for the month it doesn’t.

The other side of the comparison

Losing coverage because of a divorce can open a Special Enrollment Period on the Health Insurance Marketplace. HealthCare.gov says you may qualify if you or a household member lost qualifying coverage in the past 60 days, or expect to lose it in the next 60 days. It lists getting divorced or legally separated and losing health insurance as a qualifying change, and says plainly that a divorce without a loss of coverage does not qualify you.

Note the forward-looking half of that window. You do not have to wait for the coverage to lapse before you shop.

Three rules from HealthCare.gov decide most of what people get wrong afterward. During Open Enrollment you can move to a Marketplace plan regardless of why you’re ending continuation coverage. Outside Open Enrollment, you can switch if your continuation coverage is running out, among other listed reasons. And if you choose to end continuation coverage early, you wait until the next Open Enrollment unless another life event occurs. Voluntarily dropping it is not a loss of coverage. Letting it run out is.

HealthCare.gov also tells you to check your new coverage start date before you end anything, which is the sentence I’d tape to the laptop. And be ready to send documents proving the loss of coverage, because the application asks you to attest to what qualifies you.

One divorce-specific wrinkle: the Marketplace application asks for your expected income for the year, and savings on a Marketplace plan depend on it. Your post-divorce income is not the household income you’ve been reporting for 30 years, and the execution-date point from Chapter 15 determines whether support is taxable income to you at all. Ask the Marketplace or a navigator which items they count, and ask your CPA what your figure actually is. A single application also shows whether you qualify for Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program, and HealthCare.gov says you can enroll in those at any time, with a caution to wait for a final eligibility decision before ending other coverage.

The side-by-side sheet

Build this on one page before anybody needs an answer. Every line gets a date and the name of the person who told you.

  1. Which law applies to the plan, and who confirmed it. Private employer with 20 or more employees, a state or local government plan, a federal plan, a church-related plan, or a small employer where you’re asking your state insurance department about state continuation coverage.
  2. The two deadlines, in writing from the administrator. The date your coverage under the plan ends, where and how you must give notice of the divorce, and the last day to elect.
  3. Annual premium, both ways. Continuation premium multiplied by 12. Then the Marketplace premium you’d actually pay after any savings, multiplied by 12. For a real decision, compare premiums only over the same coverage dates; record each plan-year reset and what you’ve already paid before estimating the remainder of this year.
  4. Premium plus in-network, covered-care out-of-pocket limit, both ways. This is not a total-spending ceiling. HealthCare.gov’s definition of the out-of-pocket limit excludes your premiums, anything you spend on services the plan doesn’t cover, out-of-network care, and charges above the allowed amount a provider may bill. It is the line people skip and then get surprised by, in both directions.
  5. Your likely out-of-network and uncovered care, both ways. List the providers you use who may sit outside each network, the services each plan excludes, and ask each plan in writing what it would pay. Those dollars land on top of the number in line 4.
  6. Your doctors, your hospital, your prescriptions, each checked against each plan. Call the offices and ask about the specific plan, by name, for next year.
  7. What resets if you switch mid-year. Ask each plan whether anything you’ve already paid toward this year’s deductible or out-of-pocket maximum counts under the new one.

Now the arithmetic, using the $816 figure from the invented plan above against an equally invented Marketplace premium of $505 a month after assumed savings. These are not quotes, not averages, and not anybody’s actual costs.

Premiums first. Continuation coverage: $816 multiplied by 12 = $9,792. Marketplace plan: $505 multiplied by 12 = $6,060. The premium difference for the year is $9,792 minus $6,060 = $3,732 in the Marketplace plan’s favor.

Now add the covered-care limit from line 4, assuming it is $3,500 on the group plan and $8,200 on the Marketplace plan. Continuation coverage: $9,792 plus $3,500 = $13,292. Marketplace plan: $6,060 plus $8,200 = $14,260.

Before you read anything into those two totals, answer line 5. Which of your providers is out of network under each plan, and what does each plan exclude. Out-of-network care, noncovered services and charges above the allowed amount sit outside the out-of-pocket limit entirely, so neither $13,292 nor $14,260 is a ceiling on what either plan could cost you in a bad year. They are comparisons of covered, in-network exposure and nothing more.

With that said and only with that said: $14,260 minus $13,292 = $968 of covered, in-network exposure in favor of the plan with the higher premium.

Same two plans. Two honest answers, pointing opposite directions. Which one governs your decision depends on how much care you expect to use and where you expect to use it, and that is not a question a premium can answer.

Where to get a real answer

For a private-sector plan, the Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration takes questions at 1-866-444-3272. For a state or local government plan, CMS handles the same statute and publishes an email address for it. For a small employer, your state’s department of insurance. For plan comparisons, HealthCare.gov lists local help, and a licensed broker can price plans you may not find alone.

If you are in the middle of treatment, make one more call before you choose anything. Ask the treating physician’s office which of the plans you’re weighing they accept for next year, and ask your doctor what interrupting or changing coverage would mean for the specific care you’re receiving. Switching plans is a financial decision with a clinical consequence, and the clinical half is not yours or mine to estimate.

Write the letter to the plan administrator this week. Put the reply in the folder with everything else, and put the two deadlines on a paper calendar where you’ll see them without opening anything.

Chapter 17: December 31 Decides More Than You Think

Before you choose a filing status, find the date your final decree became effective under state law.

That one answer changes your rate, your standard deduction, several credits, and who is on the hook if something on the return turns out to be wrong. It is worth getting right before you open anything else.

The calendar sets your status, not the mood of the year

IRS Publication 504, Divorced or Separated Individuals, puts it plainly: the filing status you can choose depends partly on your marital status on the last day of your tax year.

You’re unmarried for the whole year if you obtained a final decree of divorce or separate maintenance by that last day. Publication 504 adds the part people skip: you must follow your state law to determine whether you are divorced or legally separated, and an interlocutory decree isn’t a final decree. Living apart since March doesn’t settle it. Mediating since June doesn’t settle it. A signed final decree dated the 29th of December does, and one dated the 3rd of January does not, for that year.

Separated without a final decree on the last day of the year, and you are married for the whole year, which leaves two choices. Joint, or married filing separately.

Separate returns sound safer, and sometimes they are the right call. Understand the price. Publication 504 states that in almost all instances, spouses who file separately pay more combined federal tax than they would on a joint return. It lists why: a generally higher rate, a capital loss deduction limited to $1,500 instead of $3,000, no standard deduction at all if your spouse itemizes, and a string of credits reduced or unavailable. One of those rules matters more after 50 than before it. If you lived with your spouse at any time during the tax year and file separately, Publication 504 says you will have to include a higher percentage, up to 85 percent, of any Social Security or equivalent railroad retirement benefits you received.

Head of household comes up in every divorce conversation, and in a late-life divorce it often doesn’t fit. The requirements in Publication 504 are specific: you’re unmarried or considered unmarried on the last day of the year. You also must have paid more than half the annual cost of keeping up the home. A qualifying person must have lived with you in that home for more than half the year. Grown children who moved out years ago are not that person.

There is one version worth knowing about at our age. If your qualifying person is your parent, Publication 504 says the parent doesn’t have to live with you. You must be able to claim your parent as a dependent. Also, you must cover over half of the annual upkeep of the home that was your parent’s main home, for the entire year. If you’re supporting a parent while the divorce runs, raise it with the CPA. Don’t assume it either way.

A joint return you signed in 2019 is still yours

This is the paragraph I’d read twice.

Publication 504 says that both spouses may be held responsible, jointly and individually, for the tax and any interest or penalty due on a joint return. The IRS can pursue either spouse for the full balance, interest, and penalties. That applies even if the other spouse earned all the income. Then it continues: if you’re divorced, that responsibility applies to any joint return for a tax year ending before your divorce, and it applies even if your divorce decree states that your former spouse will be responsible for amounts due on previously filed joint returns.

Chapter 14 made the same shape of point about a lender. A decree allocates things between the two of you. It does not rewrite your relationship with an outside party, and the IRS is an outside party.

If that lands badly, there are doors, and they are real. Publication 504 describes three kinds of relief from joint liability: innocent spouse relief, separation of liability, and equitable relief. Separation of liability is available only to joint filers whose spouse has died, or who are divorced, legally separated, or haven’t lived together for the 12 months ending on the date the election is filed. Each has different requirements. All three are requested on Form 8857, and Publication 971 explains who qualifies.

A different form handles a different problem. If you file a joint return and your share of the refund gets applied to your spouse’s past-due debts, Publication 504 describes you as an injured spouse. Those debts include their federal or state tax, support obligations, or a federal nontax debt like a student loan. Form 8379 is how you ask for your portion back. Injured spouse and innocent spouse are not the same request and not the same form. People confuse them, file the wrong one, and wait.

If you signed joint returns for years you never read, say so to a CPA now, while there is time to look. Not in April.

The House and the Tests to Check Before You Sign

Chapter 13 priced what keeping the house costs. This is the other half of that decision, and it turns on dates.

Start with the transfer itself. IRS Publication 523, Selling Your Home, says a divorce-settlement transfer of your home, or your share of it, to a spouse or ex-spouse generally creates no gain or loss. There is nothing to report from that qualifying transfer.

More broadly, qualifying property transfers between spouses or former spouses incident to divorce generally have no recognized gain or loss; the receiving spouse usually takes the existing adjusted basis. That is not a sale, and the details and exceptions belong with your CPA. For IRA and workplace-plan transfers, return to Chapter 11 rather than treating this as a tax-free cash-out.

Publication 504 states that broader transfer rule. A nonresident alien spouse is the exception Publication 523 names for the home transfer.

A sale is the other thing. Publication 523 allows up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of a main home to be excluded, or up to $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly who meet the conditions. The tests behind that number are mechanical. Ownership: you owned the home for at least 24 months out of the 5 years leading up to the date of sale. Residence: you owned it and used it as your residence for at least 24 months of the previous 5 years, and those months don’t have to run consecutively. Look-back: you didn’t sell another home in the 2 years before this sale and take the exclusion on it.

Two divorce-specific rules sit inside those tests.

First, Publication 523 says that a home transferred to you by a spouse or ex-spouse carries their ownership time into yours. You still have to meet the residence requirement on your own.

Second, Publication 523 allows you to treat the home as your residence after separation or divorce if you remain a sole or joint owner. Your spouse or former spouse must be allowed to live there under a divorce or separation instrument and use it as their main home. That rule is why the occupancy language in a settlement is a tax clause as much as a housing clause.

Now some invented 2026 arithmetic. The figures are chosen to show the subtraction, not to describe any real house or any reader’s tax.

Assume an amount realized of $455,000 after selling expenses, and an adjusted basis of $215,000. The gain is $455,000 minus $215,000 = $240,000. A single filer who meets all three tests has an exclusion limit of $250,000. Because the assumed $240,000 gain is below that limit, it would be excluded.

Change one fact. Suppose your divorce occurred while you owned and lived in the home, and the divorce is the main reason for the sale. Publication 523 lists becoming divorced or legally separated among the unforeseeable events that can support a partial exclusion. Its Worksheet 1 compares all three periods before calculating the limit.

Assume 18 months is the shortest of your residence period, ownership period, and the time since any prior excluded sale. Then 18 divided by 24 x $250,000 gives a $187,500 partial-exclusion limit. If another period is shorter, use that one instead. The full use test is 24 months during the five years before sale, not during the last 24 months. Against a $240,000 gain, that leaves $240,000 minus $187,500 = $52,500 of gain outside the exclusion.

Notice what moved. Not the house, not the price. The months.

There is a timing question underneath all of this that belongs in the settlement conversation rather than in April. A $500,000 limit requires a joint return with both spouses meeting the residence requirement and at least one meeting ownership. Two single filers selling later are working with $250,000 apiece under their own facts. Which is better depends on the gain, the dates, and who lived where. Ask a CPA to run your actual numbers both ways before anyone agrees to a closing date, and ask about depreciation if any part of the house was ever rented or used for business, because Publication 523 treats that separately.

Splitting what you already paid

Here’s a small one that turns into a real argument every spring.

Publication 504 addresses joint estimated tax payments when you and your spouse file separate returns. Either of you can claim all of the payments, or you can divide them any way you both agree. If you can’t agree, the publication gives a formula. Your share equals the total estimated tax paid multiplied by the tax shown on your separate return, divided by the total of the tax shown on both returns.

Invented 2026 numbers again. Assume $12,000 of joint estimated payments. The tax shown on your separate return is $9,000, and on your former spouse’s return it’s $21,000, for a total of $30,000.

Your share: $9,000 divided by $30,000 = 0.3, and $12,000 multiplied by 0.3 = $3,600. Theirs is the remaining $8,400.

If you’d rather not land on that formula, agree in writing while you’re still agreeing on other things. Publication 504 also says to show both Social Security numbers in the space provided on the separate returns, and that if you divorced during the year and made joint estimated payments, your former spouse’s number goes in the space provided on line 26.

The lines that cost people money quietly

These return items are easy to miss during a divorce year.

Withholding. Publication 504’s reminder says the Form W-4 no longer uses personal allowances. If you had been claiming a personal allowance for your spouse and you divorce or legally separate, you must give your employer a new Form W-4 within 10 days after the divorce or separation. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator at IRS.gov/W4App is free, and it is a better use of an hour than most things you’ll do that month.

Estimated payments. If you receive support that is taxable to you under the execution-date rule from Chapter 15, nobody withholds from it, and Publication 504 says you may have to make estimated tax payments. Underpay through the year and you can owe a penalty even if you end up due a refund.

For an instrument that remains taxable/deductible under the pre-2019 rules, use the current-year Schedule 1 and its instructions; the IRS can change line labels. Your CPA should confirm the reporting fields and required identifying information before you file.

The payer reports deductible alimony paid. The recipient reports taxable alimony received. Check the current-year instructions for the identifying information each side must supply.

Health coverage. If you shared a Marketplace policy and divorce or legal separation occurred this year, allocate the policy amounts on separate returns under the current Form 8962 instructions. That’s the tax-return tail of the coverage decision from Chapter 16.

Legal fees. Publication 504 is blunt: you can’t deduct legal fees and court costs for getting a divorce, including fees paid for tax advice in connection with it. One piece is salvageable. You can’t deduct legal fees paid for a property settlement, but you can add them to the basis of the property you receive, and the publication gives the example of the cost of preparing and filing a deed to put the house in your name alone. Keep those invoices separated from the rest by task, not lumped into one line that says “legal.”

Name and address. A name change goes to the Social Security Administration on Form SS-5, and an address change to the IRS on Form 8822. A return filed under a name the SSA hasn’t recorded is a delay you don’t need.

The divorce-year checklist

Five things, each with a date and the name of whoever confirmed it.

  1. Your filing status for this year, decided on the decree date. Final by December 31 or not, under your state’s law. Write the date the decree was entered next to it.
  2. Every joint return still open, listed by year. Note which ones you signed without reading, and whether any has an unpaid balance or an unresolved notice. That list goes to the CPA before anything else.
  3. The house dates. Date you acquired it, months of ownership, months of residence in the last 5 years, any period it was rented or used for business, and the proposed closing date.
  4. Payments already made toward this year’s tax. Joint estimated payments, withholding on each side, and a written agreement on how they’re split.
  5. Forms to file or update. New Form W-4 within 10 days, estimated payments if support is taxable to you, Form 8962 if you shared a Marketplace plan, Form SS-5 and Form 8822 if your name or address changed, and Form 8857 or Form 8379 if a joint return has gone wrong.

Hire the hour

This is the chapter where I’d stop reading and pay someone. Not because the rules are impossible, but because the money at stake in a divorce-year return is usually larger than the fee, and the deadlines around amended returns and relief requests have teeth.

Bring the CPA the proposed settlement, not the finished one. A property division that looks even can shift once you know which spouse carries the house gain, who claims what estimated payments, and whether an old joint return is still breathing. A CPA reading a signed decree can tell you what happened. A CPA reading a draft can tell you what to change.

Make one call this week, before the preparer’s envelope turns into an appointment. Ask for the copies of the last three joint returns you filed, and read the first page of each one. You may be meeting your own finances for the first time.

Chapter 18: What the Room Is For

Celia’s office has a round table, not a desk. I noticed that the first time, and I noticed why the second time, after mediation.

We’d started with mediation, Russ and I. The furniture took maybe twenty minutes. Who got the dining table, who got the good chair, who got the piano: choices written on a draft. Then the mediator asked us to turn to the pension, and the room went quiet in a different way. Russ didn’t know what a survivor benefit was. I didn’t either. The mediator stopped. She wasn’t a retirement-plan specialist and couldn’t advise us on the plan’s rules. She referred us to independent legal and pension help before we continued that negotiation.

Before you book a joint session: if threats, stalking, coercive control, hidden assets, blocked account access or pressure to sign make it unsafe to negotiate freely, speak privately with a family-law attorney and a domestic-violence advocate first. If you are in immediate danger, call 911.

The Department of Justice’s Office on Violence Against Women directs people seeking help to the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 800-799-7233. Call from a phone your spouse cannot monitor, if you can safely access one. The Hotline’s Internet Safety guidance warns that a monitored device may be unsafe for searching for help; private browsing doesn’t erase all traces. Ask an advocate about a safer way to communicate before using a shared device or account. New York’s court guide identifies domestic-violence cases as inappropriate for divorce mediation. Have counsel check your state’s court guidance and your circumstances privately, not in a joint appointment.

We knew which chair we wanted. Neither of us knew what the pension would pay after a death.

What mediation does well

A mediator’s job is to help two people reach their own agreement, not to decide anything for them, as the New York State Unified Court System explains in its mediation guidance. That role can be useful when the facts have been checked and the remaining disagreement is about preference.

Furniture, art, the car each of you already drives, who keeps the dog: these can involve preferences, but also ownership or value that needs checking. Where ownership, value and disclosure are genuinely settled, mediation may help you agree who takes an item; have independent counsel review any resulting settlement before signing. Liking the dining table doesn’t establish your legal right to it.

Consider an invented 2026 illustration, not a legal allocation: a joint savings statement shows $40,000, and the proposed splits are 50/50 versus 60/40. A mediator may help you discuss those proposals. The statement alone doesn’t answer whether the entire balance is divisible, whether disclosure is complete, or what either spouse is entitled to receive. Ask your own attorney to check the governing state rules before making the agreement binding. Chapters 11-14 cover the classification and asset-specific questions; don’t replace those checks with agreement about a balance.

Mediation may also help with agreeing when and how to tell adult children, where both spouses actually have a choice about their own participation. Your adult children aren’t parties whose time you can allocate. You might also discuss the timeline for moving out or contacting a bank, subject to legal obligations counsel has identified. A practical sequence is useful; it doesn’t establish ownership or release anyone from a contract.

Where it stalls

Mediation stalls where the problem isn’t disagreement, it’s not knowing enough yet.

An unanswered plan question doesn’t become an informed choice because both people want to finish. Ask the mediator to identify what information is missing and which professional can supply it. Write that down before arranging another session. The pension questions from Chapter 12 can stay in their own folder; you don’t need to reconstruct them across the table.

The same thing happens with a closely held business, restricted stock, deferred compensation, or anything that needs a valuation professional before either of you can have an informed opinion about what it’s worth. It happens with a QDRO’s actual drafting, which needs the plan’s written procedures in front of a lawyer, not a conversation about what seems reasonable.

If a safety concern emerges during talks, return to the private-help route at the start of this chapter. Don’t treat it as another valuation question for a specialist to answer while the joint session continues.

A mediator helps you reach agreement. A mediator does not replace the retirement specialist who can tell you what a pension election actually does. A mediator does not replace the CPA who can run a tax comparison both ways, or the appraiser who can put a defensible number on a business. When the question in front of you is “what is this actually worth and what does it actually do,” that’s not a mediation question yet. Get the information first. Mediate the split after.

What a lawyer adds that mediation doesn’t

A mediator is neutral by design. Neither of you has someone in the room whose job is specifically to look out for your interests and tell you when something is a bad idea.

A lawyer representing only you does that. Celia’s survivor-rights question is in Chapter 12. Here the distinction is between explaining the process neutrally and advising you about the consequences of the draft in front of you. A mediator can flag missing information for both parties. Your own counsel can examine whether accepting the proposed terms serves your interests, and tell you what still needs an answer before signing.

A lawyer also knows what your state’s law actually says about property division, support, and what a court will and won’t enforce, instead of what feels fair in the room. And a lawyer can draft or review the documents that have to hold up later. The decree itself, a QDRO, a settlement agreement: these need language a plan administrator or a judge will accept, and that’s a different skill than reaching agreement.

There’s a difference, too, between a mediator and a lawyer-mediator, and it’s worth asking about directly. Some mediators are also attorneys, and some of those will tell you plainly that they represent the process, not either of you, no matter which bar card is in their wallet. Ask the question anyway, in plain words, before your first session: are you representing either of us, or only the process? Write the answer down.

None of that requires giving up on mediation. It requires knowing which seat you need for which question.

The cost comparison, honestly

Compare written proposals, not the words “mediation” and “lawyer.” New York’s Mediating Your Case court guide tells readers to ask about charges, additional fees, session length and who drafts the agreement. Its divorce-mediation guide identifies free and reduced-fee programs as well as private fee-for-service referrals. Those are New York examples, not prices or eligibility promises for your state. Ask your own court’s mediation program what is available and what its offer includes.

On one sheet, name each proposed path and put the date beside every quote. For the mediator, obtain the hourly or session fee and any minimum booking or payment. Ask about preparation time, document review, cancellation charges and follow-up work. If the fee is per session, record how long that session lasts. Ask who pays which charges. A free initial appointment is not a quote for the entire divorce, and an hourly rate without an estimate of hours leaves the total open.

Obtain each lawyer’s review estimate separately, including review of the proposed agreement before signing. Ask whether that estimate includes an initial consultation, attendance at mediation, revisions or only one reading of a completed draft. For a proposed attorney-led route, ask what work its estimate covers too. A retainer is money paid toward work under the engagement terms, not necessarily the final cost; have the lawyer explain billing and any replenishment requirement before you count it as a total.

Add the specialist or valuation estimates the actual issues require, and the expected document-drafting costs. Identify who prepares the settlement, who prepares any separate order and whether revisions after legal or plan review cost extra. Keep specialist work needed under either path in both comparisons; it doesn’t disappear because a different person chairs the meeting. Leave an unanswered charge marked “not quoted,” rather than treating it as zero.

Then compare the total proposed paths on matching assumptions. Add the quoted session charges, independent legal review, specialist work and drafting for each. If a provider gives a range, keep the range and the assumptions behind it. You haven’t discovered a final bill. You’ve made the proposed work visible enough to ask why one estimate includes a task the other omits.

Ask what happens if talks stall: can you pause while information is obtained, what work remains usable, and what new fees would an attorney-led route require? Ask how extra sessions or draft revisions change the estimate. Timing matters too, but get proposed dates and dependencies rather than a promise that one route is faster. Neither a low hourly rate nor a short first appointment tells you what finishing will cost.

There is also your capacity to consider another draft carefully. Don’t convert that into a dollar saving nobody has quoted. Do tell counsel if exhaustion is making you willing to sign terms you haven’t understood. The answer isn’t to remove the review from the estimate; it’s to arrange the work so you can make an informed decision.

Using both together

You needn’t treat mediation and your own lawyer as mutually exclusive. The order of their work matters.

If private screening establishes that mediation is appropriate, one workable order is to consult an attorney early about the scope of review you need. Have counsel flag specialist questions before a joint session. Mediate the issues whose ownership, value and disclosure have been checked. Bring the attorney back to review the draft agreement before anyone signs it. For anything a mediator flags as outside their expertise, a pension, a business, restricted stock, get that specialist’s information before the next mediation session, not during it. New York’s court guidance recommends speaking with a lawyer before or between sessions and says you may bring one; ask about the rules and arrangements where you live.

Some mediators work specifically with each spouse’s own attorney present or on call, which is its own model and worth asking about directly. Ask whether this mediator expects each of you to have independent counsel review anything you sign, and whether they’ll say so plainly if a question needs a specialist neither of you has brought in yet.

This order isn’t a script to follow exactly. Agree with your attorney which tasks require advice before negotiation and which drafts will be reviewed afterward. A new issue can change that arrangement. Before any session, ask whether what’s on the table today is a preference question or an information question, and route it accordingly. Independent review before signing remains part of the plan, not an optional expense reserved for complicated assets.

The question that comes before any of this

The opening safety gate applies throughout the process, not just on booking day. The Department of Justice’s domestic-violence guidance includes economic, technological and coercive abuse; physical injury is not the only reason to seek private support. You don’t have to decide on the right label before describing what is happening to an advocate or your own lawyer.

Tell them privately what prevents you from saying no, obtaining records or taking time to consider a draft. Ask the advocate to help you plan safe contact, and ask the attorney how disclosure and negotiation should be handled under your state’s rules. Those are different jobs. The advocate is not deciding your legal property share, and the lawyer’s document request is not, by itself, a safety plan.

Don’t use a joint session to test whether your spouse will let you disagree. Nor should you assume that separate rooms or an online appointment make the underlying situation safe. Discuss the actual arrangement privately with counsel and an advocate before taking part. If you’ve already booked, use a safe contact route to ask how to pause or change the process without increasing risk. A concern arising after the first session deserves the same attention as one present before it.

Mediation depends on being able to negotiate freely. A neutral chair doesn’t supply that freedom. This isn’t an item to weigh against the fee estimate. New York’s court guide gives a clear warning about domestic-violence cases; your attorney should identify the applicable local guidance, while an advocate helps with the circumstances no fee schedule can address.

A decision checklist

Work through this before you agree to mediate anything, and keep it where you can add to it as new issues come up.

  1. Safety first. Have you considered the opening screen privately, including whether you can refuse a proposal without fear? If anything there applies, use the private attorney-and-advocate route before considering mediation. Don’t move to question 2 while that concern remains unresolved.
  2. What’s actually in dispute: facts, or preference? An agreed balance isn’t enough: have ownership, value and disclosure checked before negotiating the split. If you don’t yet know what something is worth or what it does, get that information first.
  3. Does this issue need a specialist’s input to even understand it? Pensions, QDROs, closely held businesses, restricted stock, deferred compensation — route these to the right professional before the mediation session, not during it.
  4. Will the result need to be enforceable or filed with a court or a plan administrator? If so, have an attorney review the language before anyone signs, even if mediation produced the agreement.
  5. Do you each have, or have access to, independent counsel to review anything before signing? If the answer is no, that’s worth fixing before the first session, not after a draft is on the table.

After four meetings, we took the unresolved pension question to Celia. She made us get the plan’s answer before we agreed to anything.

Celia’s round table wasn’t an answer. A round table is just a table. Before your next appointment, mark the unanswered item on the draft and ask who can supply the answer. Leave it unsigned until your own attorney has reviewed it.

Chapter 19: Who’s Still Listed

Two years after the decree was signed, I called Fidelity about something else entirely. A routing number, I think, for a distribution I was setting up. The woman on the phone read back my IRA’s beneficiary designation to confirm she had the right account.

“Russell Dunn,” she said. “One hundred percent.”

I asked her to say it again, because I’d misheard her the first time, and I hadn’t.

Nothing about my divorce had touched that form. Not the decree, not the property settlement, not the two years that had passed since I’d signed anything with his name on it. The account itself had been divided in the settlement — my portion was mine, full stop, sitting in an IRA that had existed exactly as long as the marriage hadn’t. But the piece of paper that said who gets it if I die still named the man I used to be married to.

I fixed it that afternoon. I’m not telling you this story so you’ll feel smarter than I was. I’m telling you because I had read my decree twice looking for a line about beneficiaries, and there wasn’t one, and I assumed that meant it had been handled somewhere else, by someone else, automatically. It hadn’t. Nothing about a beneficiary form updates itself.

Two different questions, often confused

There are two separate questions here, and the whole chapter turns on keeping them apart.

The first: what does the form currently say? That one is simple. You can call the institution, log into the account, or read your last statement, and find out exactly who is named right now.

The second: if you don’t change it, does the law treat an ex-spouse’s designation as automatically canceled anyway? That one does not have a single answer. It depends on what kind of account it is and what the plan’s own terms say. It depends on whether federal law governs that particular plan and preempts a state’s rule. And it depends on whether your state even has a statute that revokes an ex-spouse’s beneficiary status at divorce in the first place. Some states have such a statute. Some don’t. Where one exists, it may apply to some account types and not others, and a plan governed by federal retirement law can operate under federal rules regardless of what your state’s statute says.

I’m not going to hand you a table of which states do what, because I’d be wrong by the time you read it, and wrong in a way that could cost you money or cost someone else an inheritance they weren’t supposed to get. Do not rely on an assumption about automatic revocation. Ask a family-law attorney how your state’s law and each plan’s terms apply. Ask the question directly, get a direct answer, and then do the one thing that works regardless of the answer — change the form yourself.

Why “I filed the decree” isn’t the same as “I fixed the form”

Your divorce decree is a legal document that resolves property division, support and the other matters it covers. It is not, by itself, a new beneficiary designation. Even in a state where a statute revokes an ex-spouse’s status on certain accounts, that statute is solving a problem after the fact — it’s a legal backstop for people who never got around to filing a new form, not a reason to skip filing one.

And the backstop has real limits even where it applies. It may not reach every account type. It may not survive if the ex-spouse happens to also be named as a trustee, or if the governing document has specific language the statute doesn’t override. If you remarry, the old statute’s protection, whatever it covered, may not transfer to your new situation at all. None of that is a reason to relax. It’s the opposite: it’s a reason to stop treating the decree as the finish line and start treating the beneficiary form as its own separate job.

Here’s the plain fact behind all of it: do not assume a decree updated any designation. For each asset, ask its administrator which documents and elections currently govern, then obtain written confirmation of the designation or election on file. You have to submit a new form, to each institution, for each account, one at a time.

The list to work through

Go through every item on this list, even the ones that feel obviously fine. “Obviously fine” was my 401(k) rollover, right up until it wasn’t.

Employer retirement plans. Your 401(k), 403(b), or similar plan through current or former employers. If a QDRO divided this account as part of the settlement, the kind of order Chapter 11 walked through, confirm the portion that remains yours, or the new account it rolled into, has a current beneficiary designation. A rollover may create a separate IRA with its own beneficiary record or default provisions. Ask the custodian in writing who is currently named and what happens if no named beneficiary is on file; then submit and confirm the designation you intend. Don’t assume anything carried over.

IRAs. Traditional, Roth, SEP, whatever you have. Call or log in and ask specifically what the current designation says, not just whether you’ve “updated it,” since a rep’s casual “yes, we have that” sometimes means they updated your mailing address.

Life insurance. Any policy through work or privately purchased. This is the one people forget fastest, because the premium gets paid automatically and the form never crosses your desk again after the year you bought it.

Annuities. If you have one, it has a beneficiary designation separate from any will.

Pension survivor elections. This is different from the beneficiary forms above, and Chapter 12 covered why. A pension’s survivor-benefit election is often locked in once payments start. The choice may have been part of the divorce settlement itself rather than something you can simply change on a form today. Confirm what your settlement actually says about this, and ask the plan administrator in writing what your current election is and whether it’s still changeable.

Transfer-on-death and payable-on-death registrations. Ask each bank and brokerage firm whether a TOD or POD registration is available and who is currently named. For a vehicle title, ask the state motor-vehicle agency whether a transfer-on-death designation is available and effective. These registrations pass the asset directly to a named person, bypassing a will entirely, where the institution and the state both offer them. Check every account, not just the obvious retirement ones.

Health savings account. If you have an HSA, it has a beneficiary designation too, and it’s easy to lose track of since the balance is usually small until it isn’t.

For every one of these, don’t stop at submitting the new form. Get written confirmation back from the institution that the new designation is in place, showing the name and the date it was processed. A submitted form that a clerk mis-keyed is still wrong, and you won’t know unless you ask for the confirmation and actually read it when it arrives.

Why a will doesn’t rescue any of this

If you’ve already updated your will, or you’re planning to, that’s good — and it still won’t fix a single beneficiary form. For nearly every account type on the list above, the asset passes directly to whoever’s named on the form, by contract with the institution, regardless of what your will says. A will controls what passes through your estate. These accounts generally don’t pass through your estate at all; they go straight to the named person the moment the institution processes the claim.

There are exceptions, and they’re real. A few jurisdictions and a few account structures create situations where a will or a state statute can override a stale designation. But “generally it doesn’t” is the rule to plan around. “Maybe it does, in my situation” is a question for your attorney, not an assumption to lean on. If you’re working through a full estate plan, a will, powers of attorney, the rest of it, that’s its own project, and estate-planning-beginners covers it in depth. This chapter is narrower: the divorce-specific cleanup, today, on the accounts you already have.

There’s a timing reason to do this now rather than later, beyond the obvious one. Divorce tends to arrive alongside other changes: a new address, a new bank, sometimes a new last name. Each of those changes is its own reason an institution’s mailing eventually bounces or its emails land in a spam folder. The beneficiary sweep you run this month is the one you can verify in writing. The one you mean to get around to next year competes with everything else next year brings.

There’s also a cost to waiting that has nothing to do with dying unexpectedly. Every year that passes is another year a stale designation sits quietly in a file, waiting for the one circumstance that makes it matter, and by definition you will not get a warning before that circumstance arrives. The paperwork doesn’t care how settled your life feels now. It only cares what it says the day someone has to read it.

Why I’m not telling you which rule applies to you

It would be more satisfying to end this section with a clean answer. Here’s the honest shape of the research behind it: some states have passed statutes that revoke a former spouse’s beneficiary status automatically on certain accounts once a divorce is final. Other states haven’t passed anything like that at all. Where a statute exists, federal law can still override it for accounts governed by federal retirement rules, because federal law generally controls how those particular plans are administered regardless of what a state legislature decided. A life insurance policy and a 401(k) can sit in the same filing cabinet and answer to two entirely different sets of rules.

That’s not an invitation to guess which set applies to your accounts. State revocation-on-divorce rules, where applicable, differ by state and asset. Do not rely on a default rule; have local counsel identify the rule for this account and obtain the institution’s written confirmation. Ask the question plainly: for this specific account, does my ex-spouse’s designation survive the divorce unless I change it, or does it fall away automatically? Get the answer in writing if you can, and then do the sweep below regardless of what the answer turns out to be, because a correctly named beneficiary is never the wrong outcome.

A practical middle ground: some states publish their revocation-on-divorce statute’s text online through the state legislature’s website, and a handful of family-law treatises summarize which asset types a given state’s statute reaches. That reading can orient you before the attorney call, but it is not a substitute for the call. Statutes get amended, and a summary written two years ago may already be stale.

The confirmation sweep

Build one row per account. Six columns: institution, who is currently named (and the date you confirmed it, in writing), whether a new designation is needed, the date you submitted it, whether you received written confirmation back, and the date that confirmation arrived.

Start the first column with the call or the login, not with memory. You think you know who’s named. I thought I knew too.

Work through every account on the list above, even the small ones, even the ones you’re sure are fine. An HSA with four hundred dollars in it is still four hundred dollars going to the wrong person if you skip it because it felt too small to matter.

When every row has a confirmation date in the last column, you’re done — not when you’ve submitted every form, but when you’ve confirmed, in writing, from the institution, that the submission actually took.

Keep the finished sheet somewhere you’ll actually find it again: the same folder as your settlement paperwork, not a browser tab you’ll close by Friday. Scan the written confirmations into the same file as the decree, so a future executor or spouse can find the record without reconstructing it from a dozen logins.

One more form, while you’re at it

If a support provision in your settlement is backed by life insurance, something Chapter 15 touched on as a question for your attorney, that policy’s beneficiary designation belongs on this same sweep. A policy meant to secure support payments after a death does no good if the beneficiary line still says someone other than the person it’s supposed to protect.

The same goes the other direction. If your settlement requires you to carry a policy naming your ex, or your children, as beneficiary to secure something you owe, that designation needs the same written confirmation as everything else on your own list. Don’t assume the policy you bought years ago, for a different reason, happens to already name the right person for this new purpose. Check it, and keep a copy of the confirmation with your settlement paperwork, not just in the insurer’s file.

What this doesn’t settle

This chapter doesn’t tell you whether your state revokes an ex-spouse’s designation automatically. I can’t tell you that without knowing your state, your plan, and the account type. Anyone who tells you a single national rule exists is giving you a wrong answer with confidence. Ask your attorney that specific question, for your specific accounts, and then do the sweep anyway. The form you submit yourself is the only part of this you don’t have to wait on anyone else to confirm.

I think about that phone call sometimes — not with embarrassment anymore, just as the moment I stopped assuming paperwork does its own work. It doesn’t. You have to go look.

Chapter 20: What One Household Costs

The automatic payment is still sitting on the bank screen. Same amount, same date. Beside it, on your new budget sheet, the income line has changed.

You can delete a name from the household without deleting half the bills. The refrigerator doesn’t become smaller. The rent doesn’t notice.

I’ll say this plainly: a fair-looking division and an affordable month are different tests.

This isn’t the temporary spending estimate from Chapter 10. It’s the budget for the arrangement you’re proposing to keep, or the one you’re already living under. Two sheets: the first month, with dates; the first full year, with the bills that haven’t arrived yet.

Don’t divide the old budget by two
