Start with your actual proposed household, not half the married one. A lease is a lease until its terms change. A car payment belongs in the budget at the contracted amount, not at the fraction that feels appropriate for one driver.

Some spending can fall. Work out which spending, using bills and prices rather than a percentage. Groceries are worth estimating from what you buy. Utilities need an estimate for the address you will occupy. A service formerly bundled with your spouse’s account needs its own quote. Don’t assume that living alone will preserve the old per-person price.

Nor should you assume it will double everything. This is accounting, not punishment.

Include the costs of earning your income: transport, supplies or a room required for your work. Keep business costs separate enough that they aren’t subtracted twice when you calculate take-home money.

Leave room for something you intend to keep because it matters to you. A choir subscription, lunch with a friend, a modest visit to family. Price it. I don’t like budgets that pretend a person will become entirely without wants after signing a decree.

Month one: what leaves the account, and when

Choose an actual start date. It might be the day you move, the start of separate household payments or the month after the decree.

Then open the bills, contracts and bank transactions. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s Your Money, Your Goals toolkit includes a bill calendar and a cash-flow budget tool. They are useful companions to this sheet: an annual total doesn’t tell you whether money arrives before the rent is due.

Build the month-one sheet with these entries:

  1. Opening usable cash. The money you can lawfully access, less amounts already reserved for taxes or other identified obligations.
  2. Receipts by date. Each expected net payment, its source, arrival date and confirmation status.
  3. Contracted payments by date. Housing, debt payments, coverage and other obligations already incurred, using the amount due this month.
  4. Necessary variable spending. Food, transport and other daily needs, based on a realistic estimate.
  5. Transition payments. Deposits, moving charges, setup costs and professional invoices payable during this month.
  6. Running cash balance. Update it after each receipt and payment; identify the first date it would fall below zero.

A deposit paid before the first paycheck needs opening cash. It cannot be funded by next month’s surplus. A refundable housing deposit is still money tied up until returned.

For support you pay, enter the obligation confirmed with counsel. For support you receive, distinguish the amount legally due from money actually received. An order and a bank deposit answer different questions; keep an unpaid amount visible rather than quietly counting it as available cash.

State law varies on support, temporary obligations and what you may change while a case is pending. Ask your attorney to identify the governing rule and the terms of your order before reducing a required payment or moving money subject to restrictions. A shortfall is a reason to call, not permission to disregard the papers.

If this calendar goes negative, first identify the cause. A payment-date mismatch may need a timing solution. A recurring deficit needs a change in resources or spending. Don’t use a later annual calculation to erase either problem.

Year one: bring the unopened bills into view

Pick the twelve-month period you mean. If it crosses calendar years, record that. Use known renewal quotes and dates where available; mark the unquoted later costs for review rather than treating today’s price as a promise.

The yearly sheet begins with the household’s recurring payments and realistic ordinary spending. Add separately the irregular costs not already included. Carry the annual housing figure and repair-funding allowance from Chapter 13 directly into this sheet if you’re keeping that property. Don’t rebuild its worksheet here. If you’re renting instead, use the actual proposed lease and your own associated costs.

Carry the chosen coverage figures from Chapter 16 too. Identify what health-cost cash you plan to hold beyond premiums, using that comparison rather than pretending the premium is the whole medical budget. Don’t count the same health provision under both an irregular-cost line and an additional reserve line.

Make room for car maintenance, annual registrations, professional help still needed to finish the divorce and other expenses you can identify from your records. Replace guesses with quotes when possible. Unknown doesn’t mean free.

Use this year-one structure:

  1. Net recurring resources. Total the confirmed receipts for the months they will actually be available.
  2. Recurring household funding. Include ordinary spending and required payments, with no duplicate housing or coverage components.
  3. Irregular funding. Add the annual bills and planned reserves omitted from the recurring total, with their due dates.
  4. Transition costs. Show one-time setup expenses separately from the ongoing household cost.
  5. Annual gap and cash path. Compare resources with funding needs, then test when cash is needed using the month-one calendar extended forward.

Dividing an annual bill by twelve gives a monthly saving target. It doesn’t pay a bill due next week. If you’ve already put cash aside, show that opening provision and the balance left after payment. Saving into that provision and later spending it are movements of the same money, not two separate annual costs.

A quiet first month can conceal an expensive year

Consider invented 2026 budgeting figures, unrelated to the examples in earlier chapters. These aren’t prices, recommended allowances or amounts anyone is entitled to receive. Assume all recurring receipts below are confirmed net spendable amounts, after any tax provision needed for them.

Assume monthly wages of $2,800 and support actually received of $900. That’s $3,700 available each month. Contracted household payments total $2,900; ordinary variable spending is $500. Total monthly spending is $3,400, leaving $300.

That looks workable on a sheet containing only monthly bills.

Now assume another $6,000 of annual bills and reserve funding, none included in the $3,400. Recurring spending for twelve months is $40,800. Add the $6,000 and the ongoing annual funding need becomes $46,800, or $3,900 a month on average. Twelve months of resources provide $44,400. The shortfall is $2,400 a year, equivalent to $200 monthly.

The reassuring monthly surplus has disappeared without a single unexpected expense.

Suppose usable starting cash is $9,000, after existing tax and other earmarks, and separate transition charges total $3,000. That leaves $6,000. Funding the assumed annual shortfall would reduce it to $3,600 by year-end. This assumes all receipts arrive and the stated costs don’t change; it says nothing about whether particular bills can be paid on their dates. Add a separate line for the minimum cash reserve you’ve individually chosen to protect, and its funding status — distinct from the repair and health reserves and the transition cash already counted. The $3,600 is a projected balance, not permission to spend it: compare it with the separate cash floor you need to protect; any amount below that floor is another funding gap.

Now assume support stops arriving for the rest of the year: $2,800 x 12 = $33,600, against the same $46,800 funding need — an annual gap of $13,200. After the $3,000 transition charges, the $6,000 bridge is short by $7,200 before counting any protected cash floor. Find the first missed-payment month on the cash calendar and the due date it falls short, rather than averaging the loss across the year. Use the order’s confirmed support end date and your attorney’s advice to decide whether a payment is late or legally over; don’t treat an unpaid obligation as canceled, and don’t count an unsold property or an incomplete transfer as a receipt in either version.

Cash can buy time to make a change. It doesn’t turn this recurring shortfall into income. A documented $200 monthly reduction in ongoing spending would close the assumed annual gap; crossing out necessary repair funding without reducing the underlying need would merely hide it.

Name the money before assigning it a job

Beside every resource, write where it comes from, when it becomes usable and what evidence supports the amount. A retirement statement is evidence of an asset. It isn’t evidence that the same sum can fund next month’s checking account.

For budgeting, I would put confirmed recurring net receipts first. Wages already being earned, support actually arriving, a pension already paying: use their documented amounts and dates. If you receive Social Security, use your own confirmed payment, not someone else’s estimate. The eligibility discussion stays in Chapter 12; this is the line for money available to this household.

Separate hoped-for earnings from established earnings, and if your plan requires more working hours, show when they could begin, what work is available and what expenses come with it. A future job offer isn’t today’s deposit. Keep a version of the budget without that added income until you can substantiate it.

Next, identify accessible cash intended for transition costs and a temporary bridge. Give the bridge an amount and a review date. Don’t assign one dollar to the moving bill, a tax reserve and the first year’s deficit. Savings used for living costs belong on a separate drawdown line, not disguised among wages.

Then flag proposed asset sales or retirement withdrawals for professional analysis before relying on them. Chapter 14’s basis records and Chapter 11’s retirement-transfer work remain in their folders. Here, request an estimate of spendable cash after the actual costs and tax consequences, along with the earliest realistic access date.

This is a planning order, not a universal instruction to spend cash before investments or to select one account before another. A CPA and planner may recommend a different funding sequence based on your circumstances.

Keep anything contingent in a separate version: a house not sold, a transfer not completed, support not arriving. Test how the household operates without it. An asset can be yours on paper while its spending date remains unresolved.

Take the shortfall back to the proposal

If you haven’t signed the settlement, bring the annual gap and the cash calendar to your attorney now. Say what the proposal requires in spendable money and what the proposed resources actually provide. Ask which terms remain open to negotiation and which assumptions need specialist confirmation.

Don’t ask the budget to decide your legal entitlement. Property and support rules vary by state; have counsel name the applicable statute or court guidance and explain its effect here. The sheet can show why a proposal is financially difficult without establishing that the law will provide a larger award.

Examine changes in terms of annual dollars and timing. A different housing arrangement, fewer optional commitments or additional documented earnings might change the result. Use the housing comparison from Chapter 13 rather than redoing its calculation from memory. Include the cost of making the change, not merely the savings after it happens.

You may have to choose between things you hoped to preserve. Keeping everything by assuming investment growth, uninterrupted support and no repairs is not a conservative plan. Ask the planner to test less favorable outcomes; don’t add an invented return just to make the bottom line positive.

If the decree is already final, ask counsel what, if anything, can legally be revisited. Don’t assume a disappointing budget reopens property division or permits support to change. Meanwhile, identify spending you can actually alter without breaching an obligation.

Pay for a bounded review when the guess matters

If ongoing expenses require withdrawals from retirement savings, or your plan depends on a sale or payment that isn’t secure, this is a good point to request professional help. A year-one budget cannot establish that your assets will last through retirement.

Ask a fee-only planner whether they offer a limited, hourly or fixed-project cash-flow review. Confirm in writing how they are paid, whether they receive commissions or referral compensation, and what the quoted work includes. The label alone doesn’t answer whether this person knows the divorce-related issues you need examined.

Request a defined task: review the first-year cash calendar, identify the recurring deficit, and assess the proposed retirement funding with its assumptions made explicit. Ask what longer-term analysis is needed before deciding that retirement withdrawals can sustain the household. Obtain the price and deliverables before booking; a few hours may be enough for an initial review, not for every question.

Bring the proposed or final settlement, account records, tax information and both budget sheets. Tell the planner which transfers remain unfinished and which receipt amounts are uncertain. Ask for a written explanation of the funding sequence, tax questions for the CPA and legal questions for the attorney. A planner’s spreadsheet doesn’t amend the decree.

Ask the planner to mark the first month your balance falls below your protected reserve if a promised payment is late.

Give the estimate a correction date

After the first month, replace estimated spending with what actually happened, separating one-time setup costs from recurring costs and moving unpaid bills forward instead of losing them between sheets. Keep amounts already reserved visible when checking what remains available.

If the plan depended on income that didn’t arrive, contact the relevant professional before another month passes. Set the next review date around the next uncertain payment or renewal, not around when you expect to feel settled.

Tonight, put the due date beside your largest payment and the arrival date beside the money meant to cover it. If they don’t meet, write down the call you need to make tomorrow.

Closing: After the Last Signature

The pile on the table, back at the start of this book, was never really about the paper. It was about a sentence nobody in the house had said out loud yet. Somewhere between that evening and this page it got said, by you or to you, and the paper stopped being the hardest thing in the room.

Finishing the paperwork and feeling finished are two different things, and you are allowed to arrive at the first one without the second. A decree records the orders the court entered. It does not prove that an account transfer or beneficiary change was completed. It also says nothing about how you are supposed to feel about any of it on a Tuesday six months from now, and it was never built to.

What sits where the pile used to be is a file with an order to it. That letter from a plan administrator you didn’t recognize, the one on top of the stack that first evening, reads differently now. You know which office sent it, what that office is allowed to decide, and whether it needs an answer this week or just a place in the folder. Small, maybe. Not small at all if you can still picture the night when every envelope looked equally urgent and equally unreadable.

Here is something I owe you before I stop. A good deal of what you wanted from this book was a verdict. What you got instead was a question with somebody’s phone number attached to it. Was the support figure right. Was the split fair. Should you have kept the house. I don’t know, and nobody writing for a general reader can, because family law belongs to your state and plan terms belong to your plan. You asked counsel how your state’s support factors apply to your circumstances, and that answer lives in your notes rather than in these pages. It was always going to live there.

That bothered me while I was writing. Handing you a figure would have been easier, and readers like a figure. I’d also have had no idea whose state it was true in, which is the whole trouble with a confident number in a book about family law.

The part nobody warns you about is how much of this turns out to be waiting. Waiting on a plan administrator. Waiting on a court date that moved. Waiting for a letter to say yes or no about something you had already decided months earlier, while the market did whatever the market was doing and you couldn’t act on either one. Weeks go by where the only honest entry in your notes is that nothing came. Most of this process happens in offices you’ll never see, on schedules nobody shows you. Some waits were unavoidable. Others needed an answer from counsel or the plan. Silence alone never told me which.

You may still be afraid of the money. That fear doesn’t end at the signature, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise. It does change shape. It attaches itself to figures you have seen with your own eyes and dates you wrote down yourself, and it stops being the four-in-the-morning version with no edges on it. Fear with a number on it is something you can carry into an appointment and set on a table.

The advice you will hear most often from here is to put it all behind you and stop looking back. People mean it kindly. I think it’s wrong, and expensively so. You are going to open that file on purpose for years, and not to reread the hard parts. Mostly you’ll open it to see whether a form still says what it said, whether a premium changed, whether a payment landed on the day it was meant to. That’s an ordinary household chore. Closer to testing the smoke alarms than to grieving.

Russ still texts about the grandkids’ birthdays, and I still answer, and neither of those facts needed to be bigger than it is. He isn’t a villain in my version of this, and he doesn’t have to be in yours. Some marriages end with a villain in them, and if yours did, nothing I’ve written here asks you to be gracious about it. What I am saying is that you get to decide what size the remaining relationship is, if there is one at all. Nobody else’s idea of a good divorce has to be yours, including the one a friend will describe to you over lunch with total conviction, having never seen a page of your file.

One more honest thing, since this is the last page. The day it stops hurting doesn’t announce itself. It arrives as an ordinary afternoon you forgot to be sad in, and you tend to notice about a week later, usually while doing something dull like rinsing out a casserole dish. There’s no scheduling that and no hurrying it.

What I’ll leave you with isn’t a feeling. It’s the habit that carried the hardest chapters here: write it down, ask the office that actually decides, and keep the answer in writing. A good memory loses to a written list in year three the same as in month one.

So, before you put this book away: verify the current beneficiary on the account you trust least, and save the written confirmation they send you. One account, one call or one login, one answer you can point to. Then close the folder, and go have the rest of your week.
